posts.title: Why Python Is Getting Rusty?
posts.content:
Python is becoming the steering wheel, and Rust is quietly becoming the engine.

In one sentence: You’ll keep writing Python, but more and more of the fast, always-running code underneath your import lines is now written in Rust, so your tools get quicker and crash less without you learning a new language.

First, what is Rust?

Rust is a programming language that runs about as fast as C, but checks your code for whole classes of memory mistakes before the program ever runs.

Here’s the picture to keep in mind for the rest of this post:

  • Python is the steering wheel and the driver. It’s where you decide what happens: read this file, call that model, place this order in paper mode, plot that chart.
  • Rust is the engine. You don’t touch it. You just notice the car is faster, quieter and breaks down less.

Literally, that means a Python library looks and feels like Python when you import it, but the heavy lifting inside is pre-built Rust code.

Three everyday words we’ll use a lot:

  • Compiled: Python reads your code line by line while it runs, like a live translator. Rust is compiled: a tool translates the whole program into raw machine instructions ahead of time, like a book translated before it’s printed. More work up front, much faster reading later.
  • Memory bug: a program keeps notes in the computer’s memory. A memory bug is when it reads a note it already threw away, or writes past the edge of its page. Results range from wrong numbers to crashes to security holes. Python protects you from most of these. C and C++ don’t. Rust does, and stays fast.
  • Speed: here it means two things. How long you wait (a tool answering in a blink instead of a few seconds) and how much the machine burns doing it (CPU and memory, which on a server is money).

Where Rust already sits in your stack

You probably use Rust every day without knowing it.

  • AI tools: the tokenizers that turn text into numbers for AI models (tiktoken, Hugging Face tokenizers) and the safetensors model-file format are Rust.
  • uv, Ruff, pydantic-core, Polars: more on these below.

At the bottom, the GPU still runs CUDA C++. Rust isn’t replacing the maths on the graphics card. It’s replacing the plumbing around it.

The pattern behind all of it

Almost every project above follows the same three-layer recipe:

  1. A Python API. The functions you import and call.
  2. A bridge called PyO3. In plain words: a translator that lets Python and Rust hand data to each other.
  3. A Rust core, shipped as a pre-built package (a “wheel”, which is just Python’s ready-to-install file format). The common flavour is an abi3 wheel, meaning one file works across many Python 3 versions.

The result: pip install something and you're done. You don't need Rust installed. You never see it.

uv, Ruff and Pydantic, in plain words

If you only change three tools this year, make it these. Each is Rust underneath, which is why each feels instant.

uv: installs packages and manages your Python projects. Think pip plus venv (and pip-tools, pipx, pyenv, poetry) in one tool. It creates your project, installs Python itself, sets up the isolated environment, and locks versions so your code runs the same on every machine. The uv README calls it "an extremely fast Python package and project manager, written in Rust" and claims it's 10-100x faster than pip.

uv init my-strategy
uv add polars
uv run backtest.py

Ruff: checks and formats your code. It finds mistakes like unused imports (that’s “linting”) and tidies the layout (that’s “formatting”). It replaces Flake8, Black, isort and friends. The Ruff README says it’s “10-100x faster than existing linters (like Flake8) and formatters (like Black)”, with over 900 built-in rules.

ruff check .
ruff format .

Pydantic: checks that your data has the right shape. You describe what your data should look like with ordinary type hints, and Pydantic checks real input against it. If an API sends a price as "abc", you get a clear error instead of a silent bug. Since version 2, its engine is a separate Rust package called pydantic-core. The Pydantic docs say its "core validation logic is written in Rust" and that this makes it "among the fastest data validation libraries for Python."

Why Rust makes them feel instant: they’re compiled ahead of time, they can use all your CPU cores at once, and they don’t pay Python’s startup and per-line costs.

One more fact worth knowing: on 19 March 2026, OpenAI agreed to acquire Astral, the company behind uv and Ruff.

AI tools are going the same way

The same thing is happening in AI. Tools like OpenAI’s Codex CLI and GitHub’s Copilot agent runtime moved their always-running parts to Rust, while the AI models themselves are still built in Python with PyTorch. Python is where people experiment, and Rust is what runs nonstop underneath.

Why now? Safety stopped being optional

For years, the biggest source of serious security bugs has been memory bugs. Microsoft and the Chromium team have each reported that about 70% of their serious security bugs are memory-safety problems. Google says that as Android shifted new code to Rust, memory bugs fell below 20% of its vulnerabilities, with a 4x lower rollback rate and 25% less time in code review.

The Linux kernel dropped Rust’s “experimental” label in December 2025.

Rust is coming to Python itself

This is the part that justifies the title. Rust isn’t just around Python; it’s heading into CPython, the main Python program you run when you type python.

  • Nov 2025: core developers Emma Smith and Kirill Podoprigora posted a pre-PEP, “Rust for CPython”. (A PEP is Python’s formal proposal process; “pre-PEP” means the draft before it.) It was narrowed to optional modules first. Guido van Rossum, Python’s creator: “Seriously, I think this is a great development… starting to introduce Rust initially for less-essential components, and then gradually letting it take over more essential components sounds like a good plan.”
  • Mar 2026: Rust builds in the team’s fork and its automated test setup (CI).
  • Sep 2026: at the Language Summit, the first module was named: zlib (compression), using the Rust zlib-rs backend with a C fallback.
  • Dec 2026 / early Jan 2027: target for the actual PEP. No number yet.
  • Python 3.16: the target release (beta May 2027, final October 2027).
  • 3.18 at the earliest (2029+): the first point at which Rust could be required to build Python.

It’s not unanimous. Concerns include making it harder for new contributors (now you need to know two languages), and the risk at the border where Rust and C talk to each other, where Rust’s safety checks have to be switched off (Rust calls these sections unsafe). Steve Dower posted a firm -1. Healthy. Slow and optional is how you change a language millions depend on.

Meanwhile, Python is getting faster on its own too. Python 3.14’s free-threaded build is now officially supported (PEP 779). Plain version: normally Python lets only one thread run Python code at a time (that lock is called the GIL); the free-threaded build removes that lock so threads can truly run in parallel. It’s a separate build, and costs roughly 5-10% on single-threaded code. Python improving and Rust arriving aren’t rival stories. They’re the same story.

Rust isn’t magic

Time for honesty.

  • Rust stops memory bugs, not logic bugs. Cloudflare’s 18 November 2025 outage came from Rust code: a feature file grew past its limit, and an unwrap() (Rust's "I'm sure this worked, crash if not") panicked. Safe language, wrong assumption, big outage.
  • Compile times hurt. In the 2025 Rust Compiler Performance Survey, about 45% of people who’d stopped using Rust cited compile times. That “translate the whole book first” step costs you every time you change code.
  • It’s harder to learn. Rust’s compiler is strict by design. Great for production, slower for a Sunday-afternoon experiment. That’s the onboarding worry in CPython too.
  • Watch the hype. In December 2025, a Microsoft engineer’s post about eliminating C and C++ by 2030 went viral, then was clarified as a research project, not a plan to rewrite Windows. Headlines run ahead of reality.

Rust is a great engine. It’s not a reason to throw away the driver.

What this means for quant and algo traders

Trading code has the exact shape this pattern loves: you want to explore in Python, but the inner loops (indicators over years of candles, Greeks across a whole option chain, crunching tick files) need to be fast and never fall over.

That’s why we use the pattern in OpenAlgo’s own libraries.

  • openalgo Python SDK 2.0.5 ships _oaindicators, a Rust core behind 100+ technical indicators.
  • opengreeks 0.2.0 calculates option Greeks and implied volatility (Black-76, Black-Scholes and Black-Scholes-Merton) with a Rust core.
  • wars 0.1.4 is a WhatsApp client for Python, built with PyO3 on top of whatsapp-rust.

All three ship as abi3 wheels. A wheel is a ready-to-install package, so pip just unpacks it. No compiling, and no Rust needed on your machine. “abi3” means one build works on every Python 3 version from the minimum it supports onward. You pip install them and write normal Python.

And it goes deeper than our own code. When we scanned OpenAlgo’s installed packages, 16 libraries had a Rust core:

  • Ours: openalgo (indicators), opengreeks (options Greeks), wars (WhatsApp)
  • Data and validation: pydantic-core, orjson, jiter, rpds
  • Security: cryptography, bcrypt
  • AI tooling: tiktoken, tokenizers, hf-xet, litellm
  • Utilities: cramjam (compression), fastuuid, primp (HTTP client)

Most OpenAlgo users never notice. They just write Python.

Popular backtesting and trading engines are moving the same way:

  • vectorbt now has an optional Rust engine. Install vectorbt[rust] and it uses Rust kernels where it can, falling back to Numba where it can’t.
  • RaptorBT is a backtesting engine written in Rust with Python bindings. A full backtest finishes in under a millisecond on typical bar counts.
  • NautilusTrader is a Rust-native trading engine. Rust runs the order matching, data handling and risk checks, while you write strategies in Python.

Practical takeaways, no Rust required:

  1. Use uv and Ruff today. Faster setup, cleaner code, fewer “works on my machine” problems.
  2. Use Pydantic for anything that arrives from outside (API responses, config files, webhook payloads). Bad data should fail loudly at the door, not quietly inside your logic.
  3. Try Polars or DuckDB for big data. Polars is a DataFrame library with a Rust core; DuckDB is a fast SQL engine you can run from Python. Both handle large candle and tick files comfortably on a laptop.
  4. Prefer compiled libraries for hot loops. If a calculation runs thousands of times per second, let a Rust-backed library do it, and keep your strategy logic in readable Python.
  5. Learn Rust only if you want to build the engine. Using these tools doesn’t require it.

(None of this is trading advice. It’s about tooling.)

The close

Python isn’t rusting away. It’s getting a better engine.

You still sit in the driver’s seat, writing the readable code that decides what happens. Underneath, the always-on, speed-critical layers are moving to Rust. At the very bottom, CUDA C++ still does the GPU maths.

So yes, Python is getting rusty. And it’s never run better.

If you build trading tools in Python, check out OpenAlgo, opengreeks and wars. Python on the outside, Rust where it counts.

posts.title: Guess what? Now you can self-host OpenAlgo inside GrokBot
posts.content:
Guess what? Now you can self-host OpenAlgo inside GrokBot, and it can act as your Quant Trading Desk for analysis.

For years, running your own algo trading platform came with a hidden tax. You rented a server, fought with Python versions, set up a reverse proxy, and logged in to your broker every morning before the bell. Many traders gave up before they wrote a single strategy.

That changes now. Grok Bot installs OpenAlgo, runs it, keeps it updated and can log in to your broker for you. What you get is a personal quant desk you can simply talk to.

What OpenAlgo is

OpenAlgo is a free, open-source, self-hosted trading platform built for Indian markets. It gives you one unified API across supported brokers, including crypto venues, so the same code works whichever broker you use.

Inside one instance you get:

  • A unified REST API and a Python SDK for quotes, market depth, historical data, option chains and orders
  • A WebSocket feed for real-time market data
  • A charting terminal, plus OpenScript, OpenAlgo’s own language for indicators and strategies
  • Flow, a no-code visual strategy builder
  • Sandbox mode, a simulated account that uses real prices for paper trading
  • Options tools such as the option chain, Greeks, OI tracker and max pain
  • A Python strategy host and Telegram alerts

Grok Bot has its own computer

Grok Bot comes with its own computer: a Debian Linux machine with 16GB of RAM and 120GB of disk. It is always on and completely separate from your laptop.

OpenAlgo runs on that machine. You don’t SSH into anything and you don’t need to keep your PC awake. You just chat, and Grok does the work on its own computer.

One-chat setup with the grokbot-setup skill

The OpenAlgo repository now ships a grokbot-setup skill inside its .claude folder. It is a playbook that teaches Grok exactly how to install and run OpenAlgo, so every new user gets the same clean setup.

For a new user, the whole process is:

  1. Install Grok Bot.
  2. Ask: “Set up OpenAlgo for my broker.”
  3. Share your OpenAlgo username and password, plus your broker’s API key, secret and redirect URL, as described in the broker section of docs.openalgo.in.

Grok then clones OpenAlgo, sets up the Python environment with uv, writes the .env file with fresh security keys, starts the app, creates your admin login and generates your API key for the SDK. Within minutes you have a working OpenAlgo instance, and you can start asking questions straight away.

Broker login, handled your way

Indian broker sessions expire around 3 AM every night, so someone has to log in each morning. You choose how that happens:

  • Manual login: you sign in yourself whenever you need to.
  • Automated login: you share your TOTP secret once. Grok generates the code itself and logs in at 8 AM every day, before the market opens, and confirms when it’s done.

Crypto brokers don’t expire sessions this way, so they don’t need a daily login at all.

17 experiments: what your quant desk can do

To show what this looks like in practice, I ran 17 experiments on Grok’s own computer against a live OpenAlgo instance. The market was closed (it was a Saturday), so everything uses the latest available data, up to the close on 16 October 2026. Every number below comes from a real API call. Nothing was invented.

1. Nineteen quotes in one call

One multiquotes call returned live snapshots for 15 Nifty heavyweights and 4 indices, sorted by day change. TCS led at +4.89% and INFY followed at +4.61%, while RELIANCE closed at the bottom, down 0.31%.

Get quotes for the top 15 Nifty stocks plus NIFTY, BANKNIFTY, NIFTYIT and INDIAVIX in one call and show a colorful table sorted by % change.

2. Six months of candles

RELIANCE daily candles for six months (127 bars) from history(), with EMA 20 and EMA 50 from openalgo.ta and volume coloured by direction.

Plot RELIANCE daily candles for the last 6 months with EMA 20 and 50 and volume.

3. Indicators with openalgo.ta

Bollinger Bands, RSI 14 and MACD on RELIANCE, all computed with OpenAlgo’s own indicator library. The latest RSI was 48.7, and MACD at -19.91 had crossed above its signal line at -24.63.

Chart RELIANCE with Bollinger Bands, RSI 14 and MACD using openalgo.ta.

4. Option chain open interest

NIFTY open interest across 31 strikes for the 19 October expiry. The put-call ratio by OI was 1.01. The heaviest call OI sat at 23,500 and the heaviest put OI at 22,500, with the ATM strike at 23,150.

Show NIFTY call and put open interest by strike for the nearest expiry, with the put-call ratio.

5. IV smile and delta

The same chain with with_greeks=True gives implied volatility and delta for every strike, priced with Black-76 off a forward of 23,092.15. Two deep in-the-money put strikes had no traded IV and are left blank rather than drawn as zero.

Plot the NIFTY IV smile and delta by strike from the option chain with Greeks.

6. Sector scoreboard for the week

Thirty NSE sectoral and thematic indices, from the close on 9 October to the close on 16 October. Nifty IT led by a wide margin at +11.72%, Media and India Digital were next at +6.11% each, and Healthcare was at the bottom at -1.08%.

Rank all NSE sector indices by this week’s % change in a colorful bar chart.

7. Sector rotation heatmap

The same 30 indices, day by day. You can see where the rotation happened: IT jumped 5.2% on Tuesday and another 3.9% on Friday.

Make a heatmap of daily sector moves this week.

8. A three-year EMA crossover backtest

A long-only EMA 20/50 crossover on NIFTY 50 over 755 daily bars, from October 2023 to October 2026, entering on the bar after the cross. The strategy returned 22.1% (CAGR 6.8%) with a 7.4% maximum drawdown, against 18.5% (CAGR 5.8%) and a 15.8% drawdown for buy and hold. It made five closed trades with a 60% win rate. This excludes costs and slippage, is hypothetical, and is not advice.

Backtest an EMA 20/50 crossover on NIFTY over 3 years and plot the equity curve against buy and hold.

9. Correlation heatmap

Daily-return correlations for 15 heavyweights over 246 trading days. INFY and TCS were the most correlated pair at 0.77. INFY and SBIN were almost unrelated at 0.02.

Correlation heatmap of daily returns for the top 15 Nifty stocks over 1 year.

10. Volatility and ATR scan

One-year annualised volatility and ATR 14 as a percentage of price. INFY was the most volatile stock over the year at 31.3%. On current ATR, TCS led at 3.04% of price.

Which Nifty heavyweights are most volatile? Compare 1-year volatility and ATR %.

11. Returns distribution

Over 754 NIFTY daily returns there were 393 up days and 360 down days. The best day was +3.82% and the worst was -5.93%, and an excess kurtosis of 5.07 shows the fat tails a normal curve misses.

Show the distribution of NIFTY daily returns over 3 years against a normal curve.

12. 52-week range scanner

This shows where each heavyweight closed within its 52-week high-low range. KOTAKBANK sat at 95% of its range, just 1.3% below its high, while MARUTI sat at 6%, near its low.

Scan the top Nifty stocks for where they sit between their 52-week high and low.

13. Intraday with VWAP and Supertrend

RELIANCE on 5-minute bars for 16 October (72 bars), with session VWAP and Supertrend from openalgo.ta. Price finished the session above VWAP: the last 5-minute close was 1,209.60 against a VWAP of 1,207.04.

Plot RELIANCE 5-minute candles for Friday with VWAP and Supertrend.

14. An OpenScript strategy, written and compiled

Grok wrote a long-only OpenScript strategy: an EMA 20/50 cross, filtered by RSI above 50, with an ATR trailing exit. It compiled with zero errors through the openscript skill’s validator and was installed into the OpenAlgo editor, ready to backtest on /trading.

Write an OpenScript EMA crossover strategy with an RSI filter and ATR trailing stop, and compile it.

15. Pine Script to OpenScript

A classic Pine Script v5 Supertrend indicator with BUY and SELL labels, converted to OpenScript and compiled cleanly as a study. The full walkthrough is in its own section below.

Convert this Pine Script Supertrend indicator to OpenScript.

16. A Flow workflow from one sentence

From one sentence, Grok built a 7-node Flow workflow. It runs every 5 minutes between 09:20 and 15:00, buys 1 RELIANCE if 5-minute RSI drops below 30, sends a Telegram alert, and otherwise just logs the reading. It passed the flow-builder validator with no errors or warnings and is ready to import at /flow.

Build a Flow workflow that buys 1 RELIANCE when 5-minute RSI drops below 30 and alerts me on Telegram.

17. A Sandbox order round trip

Grok switched OpenAlgo to Sandbox through the API and checked the mode before every order. It then placed limit orders for RELIANCE and TCS, which were accepted in Sandbox and then cancelled. A third, intraday order was correctly rejected because it came after the 15:15 square-off time. Finally Grok restored the original mode. Nothing reached the exchange.

In Sandbox mode, place test limit orders for RELIANCE and TCS, show the order book, then cancel them.

Inside the OpenAlgo app

Grok also drives the OpenAlgo web app in its own browser, so you can ask for screenshots of the real platform.

RELIANCE on the hourly chart with RSI and MACD in the charting terminal:

NIFTY on the daily chart with Supertrend:

The Tools hub, with the strategy builder, backtesters, option analytics and more:

The live NIFTY option chain:

Pine Script to OpenScript

Plenty of traders already have indicators written in Pine Script. OpenScript ships with an importer for Pine Script v5 and v6, and Grok uses it as a first draft. It then reads every warning, finishes the parts the importer can’t translate (such as alerts), and compiles the result before handing it over.

Here is the core of the Pine Script original:

//@version=5
indicator("Supertrend", overlay=true)
atrPeriod = input.int(10, "ATR Length", minval=1)
factor = input.float(3.0, "Factor", minval=0.01, step=0.01)
[supertrend, direction] = ta.supertrend(factor, atrPeriod)
plotshape(ta.change(direction) < 0, "Buy", shape.labelup, location.belowbar, color.green, text="BUY")

And the same logic in OpenScript:

version 1
atrPeriod = input(10, "ATR Length", min = 1)
factor = input(3.0, "Factor", min = 0.01, step = 0.01)
study("Supertrend", overlay = true)
st = supertrend(factor, atrPeriod)
direction = st[1]
flip = change(direction)
if flip < 0
    signal("BUY", shape = "label", at = "below", color = green)
    alert("Supertrend turned bullish", "st_buy", "Supertrend Buy")

The key differences:

  • Version line: //@version=5 is a comment in Pine. In OpenScript, version 1 is a statement.
  • Declaration: indicator(...) becomes study(...), and strategy(...) is used when the script places orders.
  • Inputs: input.int and input.float become a single input(...), with the type taken from the default value. minval becomes min.
  • Built-ins: namespaced calls such as ta.supertrend and ta.change become bare names: supertrend and change.
  • Tuples: [st, dir] = ta.supertrend(...) becomes st = supertrend(...), then st[0] and st[1].
  • Missing values: na becomes none. It propagates and plots as a gap.
  • Colours: color.green becomes green, and color.new(color.green, 90) becomes fade(green, 90).
  • Hidden plots: display=display.none becomes the colour none.
  • Markers: plotshape(cond, ...) becomes if cond followed by signal("BUY", shape = "label", at = "below").
  • Alerts: alertcondition(cond, title, message) becomes if cond followed by alert(message, id, title).
  • Maths: there is no ** operator, so use pow(x, 2).
  • Supertrend direction: both languages use -1 for an uptrend and 1 for a downtrend.

The converted file installs straight into the OpenAlgo editor, where you can add it to any chart from the indicator list.

Beyond the platform: what Grok Bot adds

OpenAlgo gives you the engine. Grok Bot adds an assistant that can read, write, watch and act on your behalf, always with your approval for anything that matters.

  • Browser operation: Grok has its own browser. It can open the OpenAlgo app, navigate pages, take screenshots, and help you sign in when a manual step is needed.
  • Monitoring live positions: ask Grok to keep an eye on your open positions and P&L through the OpenAlgo API, and to tell you when something crosses a level you set.
  • News and sentiment alerts: Grok can track market news, score news sentiment for your watchlist, and follow sentiment on X (Twitter) for symbols you care about, then alert you when the tone shifts.
  • Knowing the API and SDK: Grok understands the OpenAlgo REST API, the Python SDK, symbol formats, WebSocket feeds and the indicator library, so you can ask for what you want in plain language.
  • Writing strategies and backtesting: describe an idea, and Grok turns it into OpenScript or Python and backtests it on historical data with clear stats.
  • Routines: schedule periodic checks such as an opening scan, a mid-day OI snapshot or an end-of-day sector report, and Grok runs them on its own.
  • Paper trading on command: say the word and Grok switches to Sandbox and runs your strategy with simulated orders at real prices.
  • Python strategies in Sandbox: Grok can write a Python strategy on the SDK and test it in paper trading before you think about going live.
  • Daily summaries: get one short summary of how each of your strategies did that day.
  • Flow strategies: Grok writes and validates OpenAlgo Flow workflows, so no-code strategies come ready to import.

Weekly upgrades every Sunday at 6 AM

Every Sunday at 6 AM, Grok upgrades OpenAlgo using the project’s own upgrade procedure. It backs up the database, pulls the latest code, syncs dependencies, runs migrations and restarts the app. It restarts only the app, never the machine, and your broker session is left alone. You get a short summary, or a rollback with the exact error if anything goes wrong.

An honest note on live trading

Under SEBI’s rules, API orders must come from a static IP registered with your broker. Grok’s computer uses shared, changing IP addresses, so it isn’t suited to live order execution.

The right split is to use Grok-hosted OpenAlgo for research, analytics, charting, strategy development and paper trading in Sandbox. For live execution, run OpenAlgo on your own setup with a static IP.

Get started

  1. Install Grok Bot.
  2. Ask it to set up OpenAlgo for your broker.
  3. Choose manual login or the automated 8 AM login.
  4. Start asking questions.

The hardest part of algo trading was never the strategy. It was the plumbing. With OpenAlgo inside Grok Bot, the plumbing disappears, and you can go from an idea to a chart, a backtest and a paper trade in one sitting.

posts.title: OpenAlgo Technical Indicators for Beginners: 127 Indicators in One pip install
posts.content:
Learn SMA, EMA, Supertrend, RSI, MACD, ATR, Bollinger Bands, OBV and MFI in Python, with free yfinance data, tested code and clean charts. No broker account or API key needed.

I’m the creator of OpenAlgo. Over the years, the question I hear most from new traders who code is: “Where do I get indicators that are fast, correct and easy to use?”

Here is my answer. Run one command, pip install openalgo, and you get a technical analysis library with 127 indicator and helper functions. It works on its own. You do not need a broker login, an API key or a running OpenAlgo server to use it.

In this tutorial we will download two years of real NSE price data, calculate the most popular indicators, draw charts, and learn the beginner mistakes that waste weeks. Every code block here was run before I wrote about it.

What are OpenAlgo indicators?

Indicators are formulas applied to prices and volume. They turn a noisy chart into a few smooth lines that are easier to read. A moving average shows the trend. RSI shows how fast price is moving. ATR shows how much it usually moves in a day.

OpenAlgo gives you all of these through one object:

from openalgo import ta

A few facts, taken from the official docs and confirmed by running the library:

  • The math runs in a compiled Rust core. The docs say there is no warm-up pause and no first-call compilation delay.
  • You can pass a NumPy array, a pandas Series or a plain list.
  • Pandas in gives you pandas out, with your dates (the index) kept intact.
  • There are 127 names inside ta. I counted them with dir(ta), so you do not have to trust me.

For this tutorial I used Python 3.13, openalgo 2.0.5, yfinance 1.7.0, pandas 3.0.6 and matplotlib 3.11. Note that openalgo 2.0.5 needs Python 3.12 or newer.

Step 1: Install and count

pip install openalgo yfinance matplotlib pandas

That is all. Older releases needed an extra [indicators] install, but current versions do not.

Now let’s count the indicators:

from openalgo import ta
 
names = sorted(n for n in dir(ta) if not n.startswith("_"))
print(len(names))    # 127
print(names[:5])     # ['accelerator_oscillator', 'adl', 'adx', 'adxr', 'alligator']

The number includes the signal helpers such as crossover, which we will meet later.

Step 2: Load free data with yfinance

We will use daily prices for Reliance Industries on NSE, which Yahoo Finance calls RELIANCE.NS. Try ^NSEI for the Nifty 50 index later.

import yfinance as yf
 
raw = yf.download("RELIANCE.NS", period="2y", interval="1d",
                  auto_adjust=True, progress=False)
raw.columns = raw.columns.get_level_values(0)   # flatten the two-level column names
df = raw[["Open", "High", "Low", "Close", "Volume"]].dropna()
df.columns = ["open", "high", "low", "close", "volume"]
print(df.shape)      # (497, 5)
print(df.tail(2))

One small trap: newer yfinance versions return a two-level column header like ("Close", "RELIANCE.NS"). The line with get_level_values(0) keeps only the first level, so you get plain close, high and so on.

My run had 497 daily bars, from 9 October 2024 to 9 October 2026. Your numbers will differ a little, because new days keep arriving. In the full tutorial script I also added three download retries and a cached CSV fallback, so it still runs when Yahoo is slow.

Step 3: Trend indicators

Trend indicators answer one question: is price generally going up, down or sideways?

SMA (Simple Moving Average) is the plain average of the last N closes. EMA (Exponential Moving Average) is similar, but it gives more weight to recent days, so it reacts faster. Supertrend uses ATR (we meet it soon) to draw a line that sits under price in an uptrend and over price in a downtrend.

close, high, low, volume = df["close"], df["high"], df["low"], df["volume"]
 
df["sma_50"] = ta.sma(close, 50)
df["ema_12"] = ta.ema(close, 12)
df["ema_26"] = ta.ema(close, 26)
df["supertrend"], df["st_dir"] = ta.supertrend(high, low, close, period=10, multiplier=3.0)
 
print(df[["close", "sma_50", "ema_12", "ema_26"]].tail(2).round(2))

ta.supertrend returns two things: the line itself and a direction flag. In my test, -1 meant uptrend (the line is below price) and 1 meant downtrend. That matches the docs, but it is the opposite of what many people guess, so always check.

On the last bar in my data, the close was 1170.30 and the Supertrend line was at 1234.24 with direction 1. That is a downtrend by this indicator's definition. It is a description of the past, not a forecast.

Step 4: Momentum indicators

Momentum tells you how strong a move is, not just its direction.

RSI (Relative Strength Index) moves between 0 and 100. Traders often call readings above 70 overbought and below 30 oversold. Those are just labels. A strong stock can stay above 70 for weeks.

MACD is the gap between a fast EMA and a slow EMA, plus a smoothed “signal line” and a histogram of the difference.

df["rsi_14"] = ta.rsi(close, period=14)
df["macd"], df["macd_signal"], df["macd_hist"] = ta.macd(close, 12, 26, 9)
 
print(df[["rsi_14", "macd", "macd_signal", "macd_hist"]].tail(2).round(2))
print(df["rsi_14"].min().round(1), df["rsi_14"].max().round(1))   # 23.9 79.3

In my data, RSI ranged from 23.9 to 79.3, and the latest value was 35.42.

Step 5: Volatility indicators

Volatility tells you how much price tends to move.

ATR (Average True Range) is the average daily range in rupees, including gaps. If ATR is 22, a typical day moves about 22 rupees. Many traders use it to size stop distances.

Bollinger Bands draw a middle line (a 20-day average) with an upper and lower band set 2 standard deviations away. The bands widen when prices get jumpy and narrow when they calm down.

df["atr_14"] = ta.atr(high, low, close, period=14)
df["bb_upper"], df["bb_mid"], df["bb_lower"] = ta.bbands(close, period=20, std_dev=2.0)
 
print(df[["atr_14", "bb_upper", "bb_mid", "bb_lower"]].tail(2).round(2))

The bbands function takes std_dev. If you saw std= in an older tutorial, that was from the old 1.0.x releases. With 2.0.5, use std_dev.

On the last bar, ATR was 22.22, about 1.9% of the close. The bands were about 10% wide, measured against the middle line.

Step 6: Volume indicators

Price tells part of the story. Volume tells you how many shares changed hands while it happened.

OBV (On Balance Volume) is a running total. On an up day it adds that day’s volume, and on a down day it subtracts it. If OBV and price fall together, the move has volume behind it.

MFI (Money Flow Index) is like RSI, but it also uses volume. It also runs from 0 to 100.

df["obv"] = ta.obv(close, volume)
df["mfi_14"] = ta.mfi(high, low, close, volume, period=14)
 
print(df[["volume", "obv", "mfi_14"]].tail(2).round(2))

A note on VWAP. ta.vwap is designed for intraday bars. When I ran it on daily bars, it returned a running average over the whole series, and changing the anchor option made no difference. So for daily data, I use MFI and OBV instead.

Step 7: Signal helpers

Indicators are lines. Signals are events, such as “line A just crossed above line B”. OpenAlgo has helper functions for that. The two most common are crossover and crossunder.

Let’s mark every time the 12-day EMA crossed the 26-day EMA:

import pandas as pd
 
up = pd.Series(ta.crossover(df["ema_12"], df["ema_26"]), index=df.index)
down = pd.Series(ta.crossunder(df["ema_12"], df["ema_26"]), index=df.index)
 
print("crossovers:", int(up.sum()), "| crossunders:", int(down.sum()))
print("last 3 crossover dates:", [d.date().isoformat() for d in df.index[up][-3:]])

My run found 9 crossovers and 10 crossunders in two years. The last crossover dates were 30 April, 7 August and 7 September 2026.

Look at the very first red triangle, on 10 October 2024, right at the start of the chart. That is not a real signal. It is a warm-up artifact, which brings us to the mistakes section.

This counts past events for learning. It is not a trading recommendation.

Step 8: Pandas in, pandas out

This is the feature that saves the most time. Look at what comes back for three kinds of input:

rsi_s = ta.rsi(close, 14)                 # pandas Series in
rsi_n = ta.rsi(close.to_numpy(), 14)      # NumPy array in
rsi_l = ta.rsi(close.tolist(), 14)        # plain list in
 
print(type(rsi_s).__name__, type(rsi_n).__name__, type(rsi_l).__name__)
print(rsi_s.index.equals(close.index))    # True

The output is Series ndarray ndarray. A Series in gives a Series out, with the same dates. A NumPy array gives an array back. A list also gave me a NumPy array, not a list, so do not rely on getting a list back. The numbers were identical in all three runs.

Common beginner mistakes

1. Forgetting the warm-up NaNs. A 50-day average needs 50 days of history. The first 49 values are empty (NaN). In my data: SMA 50 had 49 empty values, Bollinger Bands 19, RSI 14, ATR 13, MFI 13 and Supertrend 9. Always drop or ignore them before you make decisions.

2. Trusting early EMA and MACD values. EMA, MACD and OBV had zero NaNs in my test, which looks nice. But their first values start from a seed, and they need a few dozen bars to settle. That is why the first crossunder on the chart is fake. Skip the first 50 or so rows.

3. Not wrapping helper outputs. The helpers (crossover, crossunder, highest, lowest and a few more) always return a plain NumPy array, even when you give them a Series. If you try df[result] or .iloc on them, you may get confusing errors. Wrap them first:

signal = pd.Series(ta.crossover(df["ema_12"], df["ema_26"]), index=df.index)

4. Acting on the same bar’s close. A daily signal is only known after the market closes. If your test buys at that same close, you are cheating with information you could not have had. Shift the signal by one bar so you act on the next one:

next_bar_signal = up.shift(1, fill_value=False)

5. Treating indicators as predictions. An indicator describes what already happened. RSI above 70 does not mean price must fall. Use indicators to organise your thinking, then test any idea on data you did not use to design it.

Put it together: one dashboard

Now we combine price, trend, momentum, volatility and volume in one picture. Here is a shortened version of the dashboard code:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 
fig, (a1, a2, a3) = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(16, 10), sharex=True,
                                 gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 1, 1]})
a1.plot(df.index, close, color="black", label="Close")
a1.plot(df.index, df["ema_12"], label="EMA 12")
a1.plot(df.index, df["ema_26"], label="EMA 26")
a1.fill_between(df.index, df["bb_lower"], df["bb_upper"], alpha=0.1)
a1.legend(ncol=3)
a2.plot(df.index, df["rsi_14"])
a2.axhline(70, ls="--"); a2.axhline(30, ls="--")
a3.bar(df.index, df["macd_hist"])
fig.savefig("mini_dashboard.png", dpi=100, bbox_inches="tight")

The full tutorial folder has a make_charts.py script that draws all the charts in this article, including the full five-panel dashboard at the top.

Here is how I read that dashboard on the latest bar, in plain words. Price is below both EMAs and below the Supertrend line. RSI is in the mid-30s, MACD is below its signal line, and ATR is calm compared with its spring 2026 peak. That tells me the stock has been weak recently. It does not tell me what happens tomorrow.

What to try next

You have used about 10 of the 127 names. Here are good next steps:

  • Swap RELIANCE.NS for ^NSEI, INFY.NS or HDFCBANK.NS, and rerun everything.
  • Try other averages from the trend group, such as ta.hma, ta.dema or ta.kama.
  • Look at ta.adx for trend strength and ta.stochastic for another momentum view.
  • Explore ta.keltner, ta.donchian and ta.chandelier_exit in the volatility group.
  • Read the docs for each group: Trend, Momentum, Volatility, Volume, Statistical, Hybrid and Utility.

Useful links:

  • OpenAlgo indicator docs
  • openalgo-python-library on GitHub
  • openalgo on PyPI

If you find a bug or want a new indicator, open an issue on GitHub.

Final thoughts

Indicators are tools for seeing, not crystal balls. The goal of this tutorial was to show how little code it takes to compute them properly with OpenAlgo: one install, one import, and the same pandas workflow you already know.

Start small, check every output yourself, and keep a healthy doubt about any line on a chart, including the ones I drew here.

Educational only, not financial advice. The examples use past data and show how the library works. They are not recommendations to buy or sell anything.

posts.title: State of Algo Trading in India 2026: Rules, Platforms, Costs
posts.content:
Machines now drive most NSE turnover, SEBI’s retail algo rules are fully live, and nearly every big broker has its own algo platform. Here is who builds the tools, what they cost, what the rules require, and where open source fits.

Disclosure: I’m the creator of OpenAlgo. Every claim below is sourced, and the sources are listed at the end.

In FY26, 87.7% of individual F&O traders in India lost money, per SEBI’s August 2026 study. In the same year, algorithms accounted for 55% of NSE’s equity-cash turnover and 66% of its derivatives turnover, per NSE Market Pulse. Profits went mostly to institutional algo desks: SEBI found that 99% of FPI and prop-trading profits came from “algo entities”.

At the same time, retail traders have never been offered more automation. Since October 2025, almost every large broker has launched its own algo platform. And since 1 April 2026, a new SEBI rulebook has decided who is allowed to run an algo, and how.

This guide covers the market, the rules, the platforms, the prices and the money behind them. Every number comes from a dated public source, listed at the end. Where something is not disclosed, I say so.

How to read this guide

  • If you’re a trader: start with the rules in plain English, then the platforms, the pricing map and the checklist.
  • If you’re an investor in brokers, exchanges or fintech: read market size, the money and the investor angle.
  • If you build fintech: focus on broker APIs, where OpenAlgo stands and what this means for builders.
  • In a hurry? Read the six takeaways below and the FAQ.

Key takeaways

1. “55% algo” is mostly institutional. NSE’s algo share covers every participant and is not split into retail and institutional. The retail API share is not disclosed.
2. The rules are fully live. The broker is responsible for every algo order, third-party vendors must be approved by the exchange, and do-it-yourself traders need a fixed IP address and must stay under 10 orders per second.
3. Only 15 vendors are NSE-empanelled (approved), per NSE’s list of 8 October 2026. Broker in-house tools and self-hosted tools use other legal routes.
4. Brokers are now the biggest platform builders. Their tools are usually free or cheap, but each one works with only one broker.
5. Platforms are small businesses. Excluding AlgoBulls, disclosed FY25 revenue across independent platforms adds up to only about ₹76–77 crore.
6. Open source is a distinct lane. It is free, works across brokers and runs on your own machine, but you do the setup, hosting and compliance yourself.

How big is algo trading in India?

Why this matters: the headline “algo share” is the most-quoted and most-misread number in this space.

The trend

Per NSE Market Pulse (September 2026), algos produced 39% of equity-cash turnover in FY15, 55% in FY26 and 57% in FY27 so far (April–August 2026). In equity derivatives, measured by notional turnover, the share went from 50% to a 70% peak in FY25, and has held at 66% since.

Much of this flow comes through colocation, meaning trading firms rent space for their servers inside the exchange’s data centre to cut delay to microseconds. In FY27 to date, colocation alone accounted for 42.8% of cash turnover and 58.1% of derivatives turnover (same source).

What the “55% algo share” does and does not mean

The number measures turnover from orders NSE classifies as algorithmic. That includes foreign investors, proprietary (“prop”) desks, high-frequency firms, colocation and direct-market-access users, and retail API users.

NSE’s published series does not split that turnover into retail API flow versus institutional, prop/HFT and co-located flow. So it must not be read as retail algo adoption.

Two pointers suggest retail is a small part. Colocation, an institutional channel, accounts for most of the algo share. And per NSE’s November 2025 FAQ, retail API orders carry a generic retail tag (“444444444444” plus a 13th digit), but NSE publishes no turnover by that tag.

The closest retail proxy: SEBI’s study found that only about 15% of individual F&O traders (out of 84.2 lakh) used an algo even once, and SEBI says even that overstates real use. It counts people, not turnover. The retail API share of turnover is not disclosed.

Who actually trades

  • Equity cash, FY26: Individuals: 33.4%; Prop traders: 30.9%; Others: Foreign investors 14.6%, domestic institutions 14.2%
  • Equity derivatives, notional, Aug 2026: Individuals: 32.9%; Prop traders: 54.7%; Others: n/a
  • Options premium, Aug 2026: Individuals: 40.3%; Prop traders: 47.3%; Others: n/a

Institutions lean heavily on algos. Per SEBI, 372 of 432 foreign portfolio investors (86%) and 323 of 693 prop traders (47%) traded F&O through algos in FY26. Prop traders made about ₹44,000 crore gross that year.

The retail reality check

  • Individuals who lost money: FY25: 90.9%; FY26: 87.7%
  • Aggregate net loss: FY25: ₹1.12 lakh crore (revised); FY26: ₹91,685 crore
  • Active individual F&O traders: FY25: 106.2 lakh; FY26: 87.5 lakh
  • Options’ share of individual losses: FY25: n/a ; FY26: 92%

The F&O curbs explain part of the drop. These include a ₹15 lakh minimum contract size and one weekly expiry per exchange (from November 2024), and higher STT (securities transaction tax) from 1 April 2026. Per SEBI, participation fell more than activity, and index-options premium turnover recovered to about ₹82,000 crore a day in H2 FY26.

So what? Machines dominate turnover, but the typical retail trader still loses. A tool that automates a strategy with no edge only helps you lose money faster.

SEBI’s retail algo rules, in plain English

Why this matters: these rules decide which tools you can legally use and what you must do yourself.

The rulebook

The core document is SEBI’s circular “Safer participation of retail investors in Algorithmic trading” (4 February 2025). It is put into practice through NSE circulars and an NSE FAQ (3 November 2025). It has applied to all stock brokers since 1 April 2026. I found no SEBI amendment to it in 2026 (searched up to 10 October 2026).

The rules that matter, decoded

  • The broker is responsible. The broker is the principal and any algo vendor is its agent. Complaints go to the broker, which must get exchange approval for each algo.
  • Every API order is tagged. All orders placed through an API (application programming interface, the way software talks to your broker) count as algo orders and carry an exchange-issued Algo-ID.
  • The 10 OPS line. OPS means orders per second. A self-built algo needs registration through the broker only above 10 OPS. A registered algo may be used only by you and your family (spouse, dependent children, parents).
  • Static IP and secure login. A static IP is a fixed internet address that your broker whitelists, so orders are accepted only from that address. You can have one primary plus an optional secondary, changeable at most once a week. Logins need OAuth and two-factor authentication, and there are no open APIs.
  • Where algos run. Vendor strategies must run on the broker’s servers. The exception is the tech-savvy client, meaning a trader who runs their own logic on their own static IP.
  • No market orders for algos. In commodities, IOC (immediate-or-cancel) orders are also barred for algos.

Key dates

  • 4 Feb 2025: SEBI circular issued
  • 22 Jul 2025: NSE operating rules (broker-server hosting, tagging)
  • 30 Sep 2025: Glide path set; ready brokers go live 1 Oct 2025
  • 25 Nov 2025: First NSE vendor empanelment (Tradetron, provisional)
  • 1 Apr 2026: Framework applies to all brokers; several tools switched off
  • 8 Oct 2026: NSE empanelled list last updated (15 vendors)

Three legal ways to run an algo

  • Broker’s own platform: Who it’s for: That broker’s clients; Do you need a static IP?: No (broker’s server IP is used); Vendor empanelment?: No; the broker gets per-algo approval; Examples: Upstox Algoverse, FYERS Automate, Dhan Cloud, ICICI Spring
  • Empanelled vendor on broker servers: Who it’s for: Clients of partner brokers; Do you need a static IP?: No; Vendor empanelment?: Yes, the vendor is empanelled; Examples: Tradetron, AlgoBulls, AlgoTest, Stratzy
  • Tech-savvy client (self-hosted): Who it’s for: You, running your own logic; Do you need a static IP?: Yes, whitelisted; Vendor empanelment?: No, if under 10 OPS and for self/family; Examples: OpenAlgo; desktop tools such as Stoxxo

A self-hosted tool cannot, without empanelment, sell or distribute strategies, run other people’s algos as a service, or advertise performance. Doing any of these makes the operator an algo provider, and for black box algos also a Research Analyst. There is no SEBI or NSE guidance yet on bundled strategy templates, “one-click” community strategies or AI-generated strategies.

So what? Pick your route first. If you use a broker’s platform or an empanelled vendor, the broker carries most of the compliance burden. If you self-host, you carry it.

NSE empanelment and white box vs black box

Why this matters: “NSE-empanelled” is now a marketing badge, so it helps to know what it does and doesn’t promise.

What empanelment means

Empanelment is the exchange’s approval for a third-party algo provider. Vendors must be empanelled with each exchange; SEBI does not register them directly. NSE’s criteria are in circular NSE/INVG/70309, and its public list gives each vendor’s name, algo type and status (provisional or final).

White box vs black box

  • White box: the logic is disclosed and replicable, so you can see what the algo does.
  • Black box: the logic is hidden. The provider must also be a SEBI-registered Research Analyst (RA) and keep a research report for each algo.

Who is on the list (8 October 2026)

NSE lists 15 empanelled algo providers, 7 final and 8 provisional. Ten are white box only. Five also offer black box: Quantiply, Oraph (AlgoTest), Stratzy, Modern Algos and Stockwiz.

The vendors include Tradetron, AlgoBulls, Quantiply, AlgoTest, Quantman, Stratzy, Market Maya, Modern Algos, Quick Algoplus, OI Pulse, StrykeX (Stockwiz), Cirrus (Quartgen) and āagman (Koti Labs). Two others, Optibase and Futures Unchained, had no verified product as of 10 October 2026. NSE does not define “provisional” publicly; reading it as approval pending full compliance is my inference.

Empanelment is necessary for vendors, but it is not proof of quality or scale. Only Tradetron, AlgoBulls and AlgoTest show meaningful disclosed traction. Cirrus resumed only on 5 October 2026, and āagman is in beta.

Broker in-house platforms, desktop tools and open-source tools are not on the list. They don’t need to be, because they use the other two routes.

So what? Use the NSE list to check a vendor’s legal status. Then judge the product separately, on transparency, cost and track record.

The broker-built platform wave (2025–26)

Why this matters: for most retail traders, the first algo tool they see will now come from their own broker.

Because vendor algos must run on broker servers, brokers became the natural hosts. Since October 2025, 15+ brokers have launched or announced platforms, in three models:

  • Free no-code builders: What you get: Build rules with menus, no coding; Examples (launch; price): Streak (Zerodha; also inside Angel One), FYERS Automate (29 Jan 2026, free; “FIA” AI assistant from Aug 2026), Definedge Algostra (22 Jan 2026, zero platform fee), Kotak Neo Strategy Bot
  • Strategy marketplaces: What you get: Subscribe to ready-made, often RA-curated algos; Examples (launch; price): Upstox Algoverse (11 Feb 2026; ₹10 or ₹20 a day per deployment plus backtest packs from ₹99 a month, GST extra; white-labelled Quantman), Flattrade Qubit (brokerage-free, paid plans from ₹1,084 a month billed yearly; white-labelled Quantman), 5paisa AlgoSpace (20 Jun 2026, zero platform fee), Motilal Oswal STRATX, IIFL Algo Marketplace (19 Jun 2026, 100+ strategies), Alice Blue 1LyAlgos, Zebu Algo, HDFC’s 16 White Box Algos (6 Aug 2026, powered by AlgoBulls)
  • Hosted code: What you get: Write or generate code that runs on the broker’s servers; Examples (launch; price): Dhan Cloud (AI turns plain English into editable Python; no static IP needed), ICICI Direct Spring (no-code plus full Python)

Motilal Oswal’s product head said STRATX crossed 1,00,000 orders a day (March 2026). Firstock announced in-house algos in September 2026 (“coming soon”), and SBI Securities is procuring a platform through an RFP.

Brokers increasingly buy or white-label rather than build. Dhan’s parent Raise bought Stratzy for about US$6 million (April 2026). HDFC partnered with AlgoBulls and NxtOption, and IIFL sources strategies from Tradetron and Stratzy. Flattrade Qubit and Upstox Algoverse are white-labelled versions of Quantman, one of the empanelled vendors. Qubit’s plans and prices match Quantman’s (Basic is ₹1,300 a month billed monthly, or ₹1,084 a month billed yearly, excluding GST), while Algoverse sells backtest packs of ₹99 to ₹1,999 a month and charges ₹10 or ₹20 a day for each deployment.

Shutdowns: the Groww Cloud lesson

  • Groww Cloud (launched 23 October 2025) was discontinued effective 2 September 2026. This is user-reported, backed by a LinkedIn post with a Groww Support reply, and the launch page now returns a 404. No reason was published; the Groww API is still live.
  • FYERS API Bridge stopped taking new subscriptions on 5 March 2026 and order placement through it ended on 1 April, with FYERS pointing users to Automate. FYERS also withdrew its own hosted version of InstaOptions from 1 April. InstaOptions itself is a Quantman product and is still available at instaoptions.trade.
  • Stratzy stopped execution for ten brokers, including Zerodha, Upstox and Groww, from 31 March 2026, citing the exchange’s broker-hosting rules. It has since added others. Per its community team (14 August 2026), it supports Dhan, Bigul, Arihant and Arham directly, and its algos are also sold through the IIFL Capital and Dhan marketplaces.
  • Cirrus Trade paused services from 1 April to 5 October 2026.

So what? Broker tools are the easiest start and usually free. But you are tied to one broker, and the product can change or disappear at short notice, so keep your strategy logic somewhere you control.

Independent platforms, options tools and desktop software

Why this matters: if you want to use more than one broker, or need specialist options tools, this is where you look.

Independent web platforms

  • Tradetron: NSE status: Provisional; Price (user): ₹0–7,500/mo (yearly billing); free live on Nuvama, INDmoney; Traction / notes: 405k+ registered (company claim); 16,979 live-deploying users in 12 months to Aug 2026 (its research); FY25 revenue ₹11.9 cr
  • AlgoBulls: NSE status: Final; Price (user): Odyssey ₹499–3,999/mo; Phoenix ₹1,600–8,300/mo (third-party listing); Traction / notes: No-code, AI (Copilot) and Python builders; white-labels for HDFC; users not disclosed
  • AlgoTest: NSE status: Provisional; Price (user): Credits ₹499–14,999; Traction / notes: Options backtest to live; FY25 revenue ₹5.3 cr (+66%)
  • Quantiply: NSE status: Final; Price (user): ₹250–2,000/mo; Traction / notes: Scheduled options algos
  • Quantman: NSE status: Final; Price (user): Basic ₹1,300/mo excl. GST (quantman.trade/plans, 10 Oct 2026); Traction / notes: Options algo builder
  • Stratzy (Dhan-owned): NSE status: Final; Price (user): Individual algos from about ₹549/mo; All Access Pass ₹17,999/mo (Dhan support page); Traction / notes: 200+ strategies; e.g. SkewHunter ₹999, Nash Drift Option Buying ₹1,499
  • Algomojo: NSE status: Not listed; Price (user): ₹999/mo; free for life if you open a broker account via Algomojo; Traction / notes: Signal-to-order across 30+ brokers (claim)
  • uTrade Algos: NSE status: Not listed; Price (user): ₹99–4,999/mo; Traction / notes: Multi-broker

Newer empanelled vendors include Market Maya (free build and paper trading; pay-per-trade live), Modern Algos (₹999/mo), Quick Algoplus (₹12,585/mo), OI Pulse (₹1,599/mo excl. GST), StrykeX (₹49,999/yr), Cirrus (₹499 per broker account per month) and āagman (AI agent, free in beta).

Options analytics and backtesting

For many options traders, the daily work happens here rather than in an algo builder:

  • Sensibull: free for Zerodha users, about ₹1,300/month for others. It has the largest verified review base of any tool here, 4.7★ from 47K Google Play reviews.
  • Opstra (Definedge): free basic tier with a Definedge account; PRO is ₹799/month (list price ₹1,300) and adds backtesting and an options algo module. Definedge claims 2.4M users.
  • Quantsapp (PRO from ₹1,667/month on yearly billing), NxtOption (free to ₹9,000/year; white-labelled by HDFC) and StockMock (₹349–1,599/month, third-party listing).
  • Volrix (new, Pune): an MCP server that lets AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT backtest Indian index derivatives, MCX commodities and crypto perpetuals from a plain-language prompt, with 22 tools. Free plan: 500 tool calls, 2 parallel backtests and 6 months of data. Pro is ₹999/month (10,000 tool calls, 4 parallel backtests, index derivatives only). Max is ₹1,999/month (unlimited tool calls with rate limits, 8 parallel backtests, index derivatives and MCX). Enterprise is quoted on request. It is a research and backtesting tool, not an order-execution platform, and the pricing page does not say whether GST is included (volrix.ai/pricing, 11 Oct 2026).

Desktop (Windows) platforms

These run on your own PC or a VPS (a rented virtual server). They use the same tech-savvy client route as self-hosted software.

  • Stoxxo (AlgoBaba): turns TradingView, ChartInk, AmiBroker, MT4/5, Python and Excel signals into orders across 70+ brokers, with a built-in options module. About ₹750/month, a figure provided to me; Algobaba shows no public price. Traction is not disclosed.
  • TradeFlow (index options, VPS included, ₹9,999 per 30 days), MyAlgoMate (from ₹3,999/month + GST) and APEX/Omega (price not disclosed).

So what? Independent platforms buy you multi-broker flexibility and marketplaces. Analytics tools suit discretionary options traders. Desktop tools give control but are closed-source and Windows-based.

Broker APIs: the independent trader’s route

Why this matters: under every self-hosted tool, and for many coders instead of any tool, sits a broker’s API.

Many independent traders skip platforms and write Python directly against their broker’s API, under the tech-savvy client route. Broker APIs are not competitors to platforms; they are the plumbing self-hosted tools, OpenAlgo included, are built on.

Which Python packages get downloaded most

PyPI is the public repository Python packages are installed from. Its download counts (via pypistats.org, mirrors excluded, 30 days to 9 October 2026) give a rough view of developer activity across 18 Indian broker-related packages.

  • Top five: Zerodha’s kiteconnect (246,433), Angel One's smartapi-python (83,500), FYERS's fyers-apiv3 (80,272), Dhan's dhanhq (72,173) and Upstox's upstox-python-sdk (40,250).
  • Next: OpenAlgo’s Python package openalgo (28,235), Groww's growwapi (25,251) and ICICI Direct's breeze-connect (19,877).
  • Mid-table: the Noren client NorenRestApiPy (11,284), used by Shoonya, Flattrade and other Noren-based brokers, so its downloads can't be split by broker. Kotak Neo's current package kotakneoapi (10,843) and 5paisa's py5paisa (7,421) follow.
  • Long tail: Alice Blue (897), Definedge (622), mStock (381), Nuvama (341), Firstock (16th, 228), IIFL Securities’ IIFLapis (17th, 191) and SAMCO (181).
Caveat: downloads include CI runs, Docker builds, bots and re-installs. They are not unique users or active traders. Some SDKs are GitHub-only and don’t appear at all: Motilal Oswal, Paytm Money, IIFL’s XTS client, and the Shoonya OAuth and Flattrade SDKs. Smaller brokers were checked only by package name.

Which broker APIs cost money (October 2026)

  • Zerodha Kite Connect: API price (official pages, 10 Oct 2026): Personal: free. Connect: ₹500/month per app; What the fee covers: Connect adds live data and historical candles
  • Dhan: API price (official pages, 10 Oct 2026): Trading API free; Data API ₹499 + GST/month; What the fee covers: Real-time data, 5-year intraday history, depth, option chain, expired options
  • Groww: API price (official pages, 10 Oct 2026): Free trial; ₹499 + 18% GST/month or ₹4,999/year + GST; What the fee covers: Paid plan adds live data and backtesting
  • FYERS, Upstox, Angel One, ICICI Breeze, Kotak Neo, 5paisa, Alice Blue, Flattrade: API price (official pages, 10 Oct 2026): Free; What the fee covers: Kotak: free “at present”. Upstox: some features need its Plus plan
  • Shoonya: API price (official pages, 10 Oct 2026): Free for “eligible users”; What the fee covers: Eligibility not defined

In short, three brokers charge: Zerodha, Dhan (data only) and Groww. Definedge appears to be free, but that is unverified.

Zerodha’s brokerage-linked waiver. On 7 October 2026, Zerodha announced that from October it is “waiving the Kite Connect API subscription fee for active traders”. In practice, a client who generates ₹2,000 or more in brokerage in a calendar month gets 500 Developer Credits (₹500), which renew the next month’s subscription. Zerodha’s forum and support page disagree on which month’s renewal the first credit covers, and GST treatment is not stated.

Expired F&O data: a quiet but useful change

Backtesting options strategies needs data for expired contracts, which used to mean paying a data vendor. Now several brokers provide it:

  • Dhan: Expired F&O data: Options, up to 5 years (futures not documented); Cost: In Data API (₹499 + GST/mo)
  • FYERS: Expired F&O data: Futures and options (beta), about 4 years; Cost: Free API (details from staff forum and SDK README)
  • Upstox: Expired F&O data: Futures and options; Cost: Needs Upstox Plus (free to activate now; may carry a different brokerage tariff)
  • Groww: Expired F&O data: Futures and options, from 2020; Cost: Paid plan only
  • Zerodha: Expired F&O data: Continuous daily futures only; no expired options; Cost: In ₹500 plan
  • Angel One: Expired F&O data: None found; Cost: n/a

Where OpenAlgo fits on this layer

OpenAlgo sits on top of these APIs; you still need a broker account, API access (plus any data fee) and a whitelisted static IP. It then gives one interface across 36 broker plugins, so a strategy isn’t tied to one broker’s SDK.

The cost is one more piece of software to install, host and update. If you only ever use one broker, its own SDK may be enough.

So what? For coders, Indian broker APIs are mostly free. The real costs are data plans, a static IP and your own time.

Where OpenAlgo stands: the all-in-one angle

Why this matters: this is where I have the most obvious bias, so I’ve kept to verifiable features and stated the trade-offs.

OpenAlgo is a free, open-source (AGPL-3.0), self-hosted platform built on Python Flask and React, with 36 broker plugins (GitHub README, 9 October 2026). Its public signals are 2,817 GitHub stars, 1,316 forks and about 499k cumulative PyPI downloads. It does not disclose a user count, and downloads are not users.

Six capabilities in one package

In my assessment, as of October 2026, I’m not aware of another platform covering all six of these in one open-source, self-hosted package:

  1. Code strategies, including AI-assisted coding: a Python strategy host with scheduling and live logs. The built-in AI agent can write strategies using the OpenAlgo SDK.
  2. No-code builder: Flow, a drag-and-drop editor with TradingView and webhook triggers.
  3. Option strategy builder and analytics: twelve tools, including payoff diagrams with live Greeks, option chain, IV smile, max pain and open-interest tools.
  4. Key-based scalping: through the Fast Scalper companion app (Rust + Tauri) in the OpenAlgo ecosystem. The key-based workflow is my description as author.
  5. Charts, custom scripts and alerts: charting, Telegram alerts, and signals from TradingView, AmiBroker and ChartInk, with OpenScript for custom scripts (see below).
  6. Agents: an in-app AI agent (bring your own model, or run one locally) that places orders only with your explicit approval, plus an MCP server that lets external AI assistants connect.
  • Code strategies (incl. AI-written): OpenAlgo: Yes; Broker-built: Some (Dhan Cloud, ICICI Spring); Independent web: Some (AlgoBulls, Tradetron AI builder); Options analytics: Not found; Desktop: Some (Stoxxo runs Python signals)
  • No-code builder: OpenAlgo: Yes (Flow); Broker-built: Most; Independent web: Most; Options analytics: Not found; Desktop: Some (TradeFlow templates)
  • Option builder & analytics: OpenAlgo: Yes; Broker-built: Some (FYERS, Definedge/Opstra, ICICI); Independent web: Some (Tradetron, AlgoTest, Quick Algoplus); Options analytics: Yes (core); Desktop: Some (Stoxxo options module)
  • Key-based scalping: OpenAlgo: Yes*; Broker-built: Not verified; Independent web: Not verified; Options analytics: Not verified; Desktop: Not verified
  • Charts, scripts & alerts: OpenAlgo: Yes*; Broker-built: Some (e.g. Streak scanners, alerts); Independent web: Not verified; Options analytics: Not verified; Desktop: Not verified
  • AI agents (LLM/MCP): OpenAlgo: Yes; Broker-built: Some (FYERS FIA, Dhan, 5paisa MCP); Independent web: Some (AlgoBulls Copilot, Tradetron, āagman); Options analytics: Some (OI Pulse AI signals; Volrix MCP for backtests); Desktop: Not found
  • Open source / multi-broker: OpenAlgo: Yes / Yes; Broker-built: No / No; Independent web: No / Yes; Options analytics: No / varies; Desktop: No / Yes

*Per the OpenAlgo README, the OpenAlgo site and the author.

Standalone products: OpenAlgo Charts and OpenScript

OpenAlgo has also launched two pieces as standalone products, so small portals, brokers and fintech companies can adopt them without the full platform:

  • OpenAlgo Charts is a separate JavaScript/TypeScript charting library (Apache-2.0, zero runtime dependencies), designed to plug into any market-data source. Per its GitHub README (snapshot of 2 October 2026, v2.6.0), it ships 112 built-in indicators, 87 drawing tools, alerts, market replay, chart trading (order and position lines, a depth ladder) and order-flow tools. It has 126 GitHub stars and is essentially a single-maintainer project.
  • OpenScript is, as I describe it as the author, a Pine-like scripting language with backtesting, live execution through a Python engine, and alerts. It is distributed separately (openalgo-script on npm, openscript on PyPI) and connects to OpenAlgo Charts through an adapter. Adoption figures are not disclosed.

Where it sits against each category

  • vs broker-built: multi-broker and portable, but brokers win on convenience (no static IP, no server, usually free).
  • vs independents: free and auditable, but no marketplace and no empanelled-vendor status.
  • vs options-analytics tools: comparable option tools, but Sensibull and Opstra have far larger verified user bases and polished apps.
  • vs desktop tools: same self-hosted route; OpenAlgo is open source and runs on Linux, a VPS or a desktop, while Stoxxo, TradeFlow and MyAlgoMate are closed but packaged, supported products.
  • vs NSE-empanelled vendors: none of the 15 is open source. They can host and distribute algos; OpenAlgo, by design, cannot.

The trade-offs, plainly

  • Setup and hosting effort: install, run on your machine or a VPS, and get a static IP whitelisted. Dhan Cloud, FYERS Automate and ICICI Spring need none of that.
  • No marketplace, no empanelment: this keeps it within the self-use route, but there are no ready-made strategies to subscribe to.
  • Compliance is on you: under 10 OPS, no market orders for algos, self and family only.
  • No disclosed user count and no paid support tier in the repository.

One outside signal: HDFC Sky published an OpenAlgo setup guide (28 August 2026).

So what? OpenAlgo fits people who value control, portability and zero licence cost, and who are comfortable running software. If you want something that just works out of the box, a broker or vendor platform will suit you better.

The pricing landscape

Why this matters: prices range from free to ₹17,999 a month, and the most expensive tool is not automatically the best.

  • Broker-built: Typical price (user): Free to about ₹1,300/mo; marketplaces from ~₹549/mo; Examples: FYERS Automate, Algostra, AlgoSpace (free); Algoverse ₹10 to ₹20/day per deployment plus packs from ₹99/mo; Qubit from ₹1,084/mo (yearly); Dhan from ₹549, all-access ₹17,999
  • Independent, empanelled: Typical price (user): ₹250–7,500/mo (Quick Algoplus ₹12,585); Examples: Quantiply, Tradetron, Quantman ₹1,300, AlgoBulls
  • Independent, not empanelled: Typical price (user): ₹99–4,999/mo; Examples: uTrade, Algomojo ₹999
  • Options analytics: Typical price (user): Free to ~₹2,500/mo; Examples: Sensibull, Opstra PRO ₹799, Quantsapp, Volrix MCP from ₹999
  • Desktop: Typical price (user): ₹750–9,999/mo; Examples: Stoxxo ~₹750, MyAlgoMate ₹3,999, TradeFlow ₹9,999
  • Open source, self-hosted: Typical price (user): Free, plus your VPS/static IP and any broker data fee; Examples: OpenAlgo
  • Broker APIs: Typical price (user): Mostly free; Zerodha ₹500, Dhan Data ₹499, Groww ₹499 (+GST); Examples: Kite Connect, DhanHQ, Groww API

Prices for several broker products (ICICI Spring, Motilal STRATX, IIFL, HDFC algos, Dhan Cloud credits) are not published.

So what? Compare total cost, not the sticker price. “Free” broker tools are paid for out of your brokerage.

The money: market size and what platforms earn

Why this matters: the size of the revenue pool tells you which tools can survive and who funds the “free” ones.

The revenue pool (analyst estimates)

My FY26 base-case estimate of all yearly revenue tied to algo/API trading in India is about ₹12,344 crore (US$1.28B), in a range of ₹10,342–14,322 crore. These are estimates built from sourced inputs, not reported figures.

This is not a retail number. About 87% of the total is exchange fees and colocation on all algo flow, which is mostly institutional. Retail algo/API brokerage is estimated at about ₹1,377 crore, using a 10% assumption because the real share is undisclosed. Retail tooling spend is about ₹212 crore.

The part independent platforms can realistically go after (the SAM, or serviceable market) is about ₹463 crore, in a range from ₹178 crore to just under ₹1,000 crore. Roughly 60% of that is broker revenue-share, which is a partner channel rather than a pool platforms win from brokers.

What platforms actually earn

  • Grew in FY25: AlgoTest (+66%), Quantman (+26%), uTrade (+17%).
  • Shrank in FY25: Sensibull (−29%), Quantsapp (−30%), Quantiply (−22.5%).
  • Outlier: AlgoBulls reported ₹356.3 crore (consolidated) but is loss-making, and the nature of its revenue is not disclosed, so it isn’t comparable.
  • Not disclosed: broker-built platform revenue, Stratzy (only “under ₹10 crore”), Algomojo, Stoxxo, desktop tools and most newer vendors. OpenAlgo earns nothing by design.
Excluding AlgoBulls, the disclosed independent pool is only about ₹76–77 crore.

So what? Retail algo tooling is a small business that is getting squeezed. Free broker tools set the price at zero, and most of the money is in brokerage and exchange fees.

The investor angle

Why this matters: algo trading changes how exchanges, brokers and fintechs make money.

Not financial advice. This section summarises public, sourced data; it is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

Exchanges earn most of the money

  • NSE revenue from operations / transaction charges: Figure: ₹16,601 cr / ₹13,057 cr (options ₹9,997.5 cr); Source: NSE IPO coverage (Upstox News)
  • NSE colocation: Figure: 1,680 racks; revenue about ₹1,330 cr (7% of revenue); Source: PL Capital
  • NSE share of index-options premium: Figure: 72% in FY26; about 65% FY27 YTD; Source: PL Capital
  • BSE revenue / equity-derivatives revenue: Figure: ₹5,148 cr (+59%) / ₹3,134 cr; Source: BusinessLine

NSE’s IPO (an offer for sale) opened on 17 September 2026 at a price band of ₹1,700–1,785. Its disclosures are now the best public data on the exchange-fee pool. BSE gaining share in index options is the competitive story to follow.

Brokers: algo tools are a loss-leader for F&O flow

  • Zerodha FY26: revenue ₹8,847 crore, profit ₹4,283 crore, brokerage ₹2,738 crore (−11%). Its net income from exchange transaction-charge rebates fell from ₹400 crore to zero after the rebates ended.
  • Groww FY26: revenue ₹4,644 crore, with equity derivatives 55% of Q4 revenue. Its F&O user penetration fell from 18% (November 2024) to 10% (Q4 FY26).
  • Angel One, Q4 FY26: 430.66 million orders and a 21.6% share of option premium.
  • Distribution: NSE had 4.61 crore active clients in September 2026. Groww led with 134.5 lakh, then Zerodha (67.9 lakh) and Angel One (67.6 lakh).

Brokers give algo platforms away for free, or nearly free, to keep active F&O traders and their brokerage. They also buy capability rather than build it, as the Raise–Stratzy deal (about US$6 million) shows.

Fintech platforms: small, regulated, consolidating

  • Disclosed independent revenue is small, and several leaders shrank in FY25 (see the previous section).
  • Only 15 vendors are empanelled; two have no verified product, and several are paused or in beta.
  • Regulation adds fixed costs: empanelment, RA registration for black box, mock sessions and finfluencer rules. From 1 July 2026, educational content may use only price data at least 30 days old.

So what? The money in Indian algo trading is concentrated in exchange fees, brokerage and institutional trading profits. Retail tooling is a feature that brokers fund out of order flow, and independent vendors have to justify their price against “free”.

Risks and a checklist for choosing a platform

Why this matters: the tool is the easy part; avoiding the expensive mistakes is harder.

Risks

  • Strategy risk beats tool risk: automation magnifies whatever edge you have, or don’t have.
  • Platform risk: tools get switched off (Groww Cloud, FYERS API Bridge) and vendors change which brokers they support (Stratzy stopped ten brokers in March 2026 and has since added others).
  • Compliance risk for self-hosters, who carry the rules themselves.
  • Cost creep: higher STT from April 2026, plus data, VPS and per-algo fees.

Checklist

  1. Route: broker in-house, empanelled vendor (check NSE’s list), or self-hosted?
  2. Lock-in: does it work with more than one broker, and what happens if the product is shut?
  3. White or black box: can you see and change the logic?
  4. Total cost: platform + per-algo + API/data + VPS/static IP + GST + brokerage + STT.
  5. Testing: backtest, paper trading and a sandbox before going live.
  6. Execution controls: limit-order handling, order slicing, risk limits, a kill switch.
  7. Transparency: disclosed charges, no return claims, a clear grievance route (your broker).
  8. Track record: verifiable traction (filings, store reviews), not just claims.
  9. Portability: can you export strategies and logs?
  10. Support: who fixes it on expiry morning?

So what? If a tool fails three or more of these checks, keep looking.

What this means for you

For traders

  • Zero setup: start with your broker’s platform, and keep a copy of your logic outside it.
  • Ready-made strategies: empanelled vendors or broker marketplaces; read the RA disclosures for black box.
  • Manual options trading: an analytics tool may be all you need.
  • Coding or multi-broker: self-hosted (open source or desktop), at the cost of setup and compliance.
  • Always: paper trade first, size small, and remember “55% algo” does not mean retail bots are winning.

For investors

  • The most durable money sits with exchanges and large brokers, not with retail tool vendors (see the investor angle).
  • Watch BSE’s options share, broker F&O revenue mix, and whether brokers keep buying algo vendors.

For fintech builders

  • Brokers are partners, not rivals: their APIs are your supply, and revenue-share is the main reachable pool.
  • The real competition is free broker tools, and brokers increasingly buy or white-label rather than build.
  • Empanelment is table stakes for hosted vendors, not a moat.
  • Open lanes: broker-agnostic agent/MCP layers, compliance tooling (static-IP checks, OPS limiters, audit logs), engines for mid-size brokers, managed hosting for self-hosters, and embeddable components such as charting and scripting.

What to watch next

  • More broker launches and deals: Firstock’s in-house algos, SBI Securities’ RFP, more white-label partnerships.
  • NSE’s empanelled list: provisional vendors moving to final; whether Optibase and Futures Unchained ship products.
  • SEBI guidance on AI-generated strategies and community templates.
  • FY26 filings for Tradetron, AlgoTest, Sensibull and others, from late 2026.
  • Jane Street vs SEBI: the Securities Appellate Tribunal is due to rule on 21 October 2026 (per Mint).
  • Static-IP friction: whether brokers or exchanges ease it for self-hosters.

FAQ

Is algo trading legal in India? Yes. Since 1 April 2026, SEBI’s retail algo framework applies to all brokers. Your algo must run through an approved route: the broker’s own platform, an NSE-empanelled vendor on broker servers, or your own logic on a whitelisted static IP under 10 orders per second, for self and family use.

What is NSE empanelment? It is the exchange’s approval for third-party algo providers, whose algos then run on broker servers. As of NSE’s list of 8 October 2026, 15 vendors are empanelled (7 final, 8 provisional).

What is the difference between white box and black box algos? A white box algo’s logic is disclosed. A black box algo’s logic is hidden, so its provider must also be a SEBI-registered Research Analyst with a research report for each algo.

Does “55% of NSE turnover is algo” mean most retail traders use algos? No. The figure covers all participants (FPIs, prop/HFT, colocation and retail) and NSE does not split it by retail versus institutional. The retail API share is not disclosed; SEBI’s closest proxy is that about 15% of individual F&O traders used an algo at least once, which SEBI says overstates real use.

Do I need a static IP for algo trading? Only if you run your own algo. If you use a broker’s platform or an empanelled vendor running on broker servers, the broker’s server IP is used.

Which is the best algo trading platform in India? There is no single best one. Broker tools are simplest; empanelled independents such as Tradetron or AlgoBulls offer multi-broker no-code and marketplaces; Sensibull or Opstra suit options work; self-hosted tools offer control. Use the checklist.

Is OpenAlgo SEBI-registered or NSE-empanelled? No. It is open-source software you run yourself under the tech-savvy client route. It doesn’t need empanelment for self-use, and it cannot distribute strategies.

How much does algo trading cost in India? From free (most broker no-code tools, open source) to ₹250–7,500/month for most empanelled platforms and ₹750–9,999/month for desktop tools, with outliers up to ₹17,999/month. See the pricing table, and add brokerage, STT, GST, data and any VPS.

Do broker APIs cost money? Mostly no. Zerodha (₹500/month for Kite Connect with data, credited back from October 2026 if you generate ₹2,000+ brokerage in a month), Dhan (₹499 + GST for data) and Groww (₹499 + GST) charge; the other brokers checked are free.

Can I get historical data for expired options through broker APIs? At some brokers: Dhan, FYERS (beta), Upstox (Plus plan) and Groww (paid plan). Zerodha offers daily futures data only. See the expired-data table above.
