posts.title: OpenScript: An Open Source Custom Scripting Engine to Build Your Own Indicators and Strategies
posts.content:
Have you ever wondered why the indicator you spent weeks perfecting only works on one website?

Every trader who writes their own indicators runs into the same wall. You write a script in one platform’s language. It lives on that platform’s servers, draws only on that platform’s charts, and trades only with the brokers that platform chooses to support. Change the platform, and your work stays behind. Want to trade the same idea through your own broker? Rewrite it. Want to run it on your own server? Rewrite it again. Over the years, traders end up locked in, not because the platform is the best, but because leaving means starting from zero.

Now imagine the opposite. A scripting language that is open source, that you can run anywhere, and that anyone, a trader, a developer, a broker, a startup, can use to build their own charting engine with custom scripts. Your indicators and strategies belong to you, not to a website.

That is OpenScript. And it is not a prototype. It already powers the chart based trading section of OpenAlgo today.

What is OpenScript?

OpenScript is an open source custom scripting engine for trading. If you have used Pine Script on TradingView or AFL on Amibroker, the idea will feel familiar: you describe a calculation bar by bar, and the engine draws it, tests it or trades it for you.

There are two kinds of script:

  • A study is an indicator. It draws lines, bands and labels on your chart. It never places an order.
  • A strategy also decides when to buy and when to exit. You can backtest it, run it in sandbox mode, and trade it live.

The difference between the two starts with one word at the top of the script: study(...) or strategy(...).

Build your own indicators: HalfTrend as an example

HalfTrend is a popular trend indicator. It holds a flat level through noise and only turns when the other side of the recent range gives way. Blue while the trend is up, red while it is down, with a shaded channel and a Buy or Sell label on every flip.

Here is the complete HalfTrend indicator in OpenScript. Copy it, paste it into the Scripts panel on OpenAlgo’s Trading page (or the playground on openalgo.in/script), press Save, and it is on your chart:

// HalfTrend: a trend level that holds flat through noise and turns only when
// the other side of the range gives way. Blue while the trend is up, red while
// it is down, with a shaded channel and a label on every flip.
version 1
 
study("HalfTrend", overlay = true, precision = 2)
 
amplitude = input(2, "Amplitude", min = 1, max = 100)
channelDev = input(2, "Channel deviation", min = 0, max = 20)
atrLen = input(100, "ATR length", min = 1, max = 500)
 
half = atr(atrLen) / 2
dev = channelDev * half
rollHigh = highest(high, amplitude)
rollLow = lowest(low, amplitude)
meanHigh = sma(high, amplitude)
meanLow = sma(low, amplitude)
prevHigh = bar.isFirst ? high : high[1]
prevLow = bar.isFirst ? low : low[1]
 
// trend is 0 while up and 1 while down; armed is the flip being watched for.
var trend = 0
var armed = 0
var maxLow = low
var minHigh = high
var upLevel = low
var downLevel = high
 
wasTrend = bar.isFirst ? -1 : trend
 
if armed == 1
    maxLow = max(orElse(rollLow, maxLow), maxLow)
    if not isNone(meanHigh) and meanHigh < maxLow and close < prevLow
        trend = 1
        armed = 0
        minHigh = orElse(rollHigh, high)
else
    minHigh = min(orElse(rollHigh, minHigh), minHigh)
    if not isNone(meanLow) and meanLow > minHigh and close > prevHigh
        trend = 0
        armed = 1
        maxLow = orElse(rollLow, low)
 
flipUp = trend == 0 and wasTrend == 1
flipDown = trend == 1 and wasTrend == 0
 
// On a flip the new level starts where the other side ended, so it steps.
if trend == 0
    upLevel = flipUp ? downLevel : wasTrend == -1 ? maxLow : max(maxLow, upLevel)
else
    downLevel = flipDown ? upLevel : wasTrend == -1 ? minHigh : min(minHigh, downLevel)
 
ht = trend == 0 ? upLevel : downLevel
 
upLine = plot(trend == 0 ? ht : none, "Up trend", #2962ff, width = 2)
downLine = plot(trend == 1 ? ht : none, "Down trend", #ef5350, width = 2)
upEdge = plot(trend == 0 ? ht - dev : none, "Channel low", fade(#2962ff, 55), width = 1)
downEdge = plot(trend == 1 ? ht + dev : none, "Channel high", fade(#ef5350, 55), width = 1)
fill(upLine, upEdge, fade(#2962ff, 82))
fill(downLine, downEdge, fade(#ef5350, 82))
 
if flipUp
    signal("Buy", #2962ff, at = "below", shape = "label")
 
if flipDown
    signal("Sell", #ef5350, at = "above", shape = "label")

Even without knowing the language, most of it reads like plain English: take the inputs, calculate the ATR and the recent highs and lows, decide whether the trend has flipped, then draw the lines, the shaded channel and the Buy and Sell labels.

It tells you exactly what is wrong

When a community member first shared this script, it did not compile. That turned out to be useful.

The first line started with a single slash (/ HalfTrend) instead of the two slashes that mark a comment (// HalfTrend). A tiny typo, but OpenScript caught it before anything reached the chart and reported exactly where it was:

  • OS1022: an expression was expected after /
  • OS2001: HalfTrend is not defined
  • OS1021: the version line must come first

All three come from that one missing slash. Add it, press Save, and the status bar changes to “Ready”. This is the most important habit OpenScript builds: a script with a mistake never runs. It does not quietly draw the wrong line or place a wrong order. It stops and tells you why.

Does the custom version match the real thing?

OpenAlgo’s chart already ships a built-in HalfTrend. So we applied both, the built-in one and the custom OpenScript one, on the same AXISBANK chart. The lines lie exactly on top of each other, the Buy and Sell labels appear on the same bars, and the values in the legend match. The custom script is a faithful copy of the indicator.

This is a good habit for any trader bringing an indicator from another platform: rebuild it, then check it against a version you trust before you rely on it.

Help while you write

You do not need to memorise anything. The OpenScript editor on openalgo.in/script checks your script as you type, and hovering over any function shows what it does and what it expects.

Your first strategy: a simple EMA crossover

An indicator shows you what the market is doing. A strategy acts on it. The classic starting point is the moving average crossover: buy when a fast EMA crosses above a slow EMA, and exit when it crosses back below. Here is the complete long only version:

// EMA Crossover: go long when the fast EMA crosses above the slow EMA,
// and exit the long when it crosses back below. Long only, never short.
version 1
 
strategy("EMA Crossover, long only", overlay = true, precision = 2,
         capital = 100000, qty = input(10, "Quantity", min = 1), qtyType = "units",
         product = "intraday", fillOn = "nextOpen")
 
fastLen = input(9, "Fast EMA", min = 1, max = 200)
slowLen = input(21, "Slow EMA", min = 1, max = 500)
 
fast = ema(close, fastLen)
slow = ema(close, slowLen)
 
plot(fast, "Fast EMA", #2962ff, width = 2)
plot(slow, "Slow EMA", #ff9800, width = 2)
 
// Long entry: fast EMA crosses above slow EMA while we have no position.
if crossUp(fast, slow) and pos.isFlat
    buy()
 
// Long exit: fast EMA crosses below slow EMA while we are long.
if crossDown(fast, slow) and pos.isLong
    close()

Read it like a sentence:

  • The first line says this is a strategy, not a study, and sets how to trade it the way a trader thinks: starting capital, quantity, product type (intraday), and fill at the next bar's open.
  • The inputs are the 9 and 21 period EMAs. Change them from the settings without touching the code.
  • The two plots draw both EMAs on your chart, so you can see every crossover.
  • Long entry: if the fast EMA crosses above the slow EMA and you have no position, buy().
  • Long exit: if the fast EMA crosses below the slow EMA and you are long, close().

The checks pos.isFlat and pos.isLong make sure it never buys twice or sells what it does not hold. That is the whole strategy: about twenty lines, most of them comments and settings.

Backtesting in your browser

Press the play button next to a strategy and OpenAlgo runs it over the bars on your chart and opens a full report: net profit, win rate, drawdown, every trade with its entry and exit, and every fill marked on the chart. It runs entirely in your browser, on thousands of bars in a fraction of a second, and nothing is sent to your broker. You can try different EMA lengths, a different timeframe or a different exit, and test again in seconds, with no money at risk.

Execution: sandbox first, then live

When a strategy is ready, you deploy it from the Strategies panel. A deployed strategy no longer runs in your browser. It runs on your OpenAlgo server, bar by bar, and places its orders through the same order path as every other OpenAlgo order.

  • In analyzer mode (sandbox mode), those orders go to OpenAlgo’s sandbox with virtual funds. You can watch your strategy trade live market data without risking a rupee.
  • In live mode, the same orders go to your broker.

The strategy does not change between the two. You flip the mode, not the code. The thing you tested is the thing you trade.

How it works, in plain language

You do not need to know any of this to use OpenScript, but it explains why you can trust it.

When you press Save, OpenScript does three things in your browser, in about 10 milliseconds:

  1. It reads your script, word by word.
  2. It checks it for mistakes: a typo, a name that does not exist, a setting that is out of range. If it finds any, it stops and shows you the line and the fix.
  3. It seals it into a recipe. The result is not a program that can do anything it likes. It is a fixed list of calculations, stored as data, with a fingerprint of your original script. It cannot open files, reach the internet, or run anything that is not an OpenScript calculation.

That sealed recipe is then run by two engines that follow the same rules: one in the browser (for the chart and the backtest) and one on the server (for the live strategy). Because both engines run the same recipe, what you see on the chart, what you backtest, and what you trade are the same calculation. They cannot quietly drift apart.

A few details that matter to traders:

  • No fake values at the start. A 21 period EMA has no value until enough bars exist. OpenScript leaves it empty rather than pretending it is zero, so early signals are not invented.
  • Clear, numbered errors. Every problem has a code (like OS2001) and a suggested fix, so you can search for it or ask for help.
  • A large library. Moving averages, ATR, RSI, highest and lowest, crossovers and hundreds more are built in, with the list growing each release.

Build your own charting engine

This is where OpenScript is different from every closed trading language. It is not a feature locked inside one product. It is an engine you can take and build on.

  • The engines are published packages. JavaScript on npm (openalgo-script) for charts and browsers, and Python on PyPI (openscript) for servers, research notebooks and automation.
  • The language has a published specification, so the rules are written down, not hidden inside one product.
  • A conformance test suite checks that every engine produces the same numbers on the same tests. That is how OpenAlgo’s browser engine and server engine stay in agreement, and how anyone else can build a compatible one.

OpenAlgo’s own chart based trading section is the proof: the charts, the custom indicators, the in-browser backtest and the deployed strategies you saw above are all built on these same public engines. A trader or developer can use the same pieces to add custom scripting to their own charting app, dashboard or trading tool.

Built for commercial use: businesses, brokers and web portals

OpenScript is released under the Apache 2.0 licence, which is designed to allow commercial use. That opens the door well beyond individual traders:

  • Brokers can offer custom indicators and strategies on their own trading terminals and charts, without licensing a closed scripting language from someone else.
  • Web portals and fintech startups can add a scripting layer to their charting, screening or strategy products, and let their users write their own logic.
  • Businesses and trading desks can standardise on one language for research, backtesting and execution, and keep full control of where their scripts run.

And because every compatible engine follows the same specification, a script written on one platform can run on another. For traders, that means no more lock-in. For businesses, it means building on a shared standard instead of reinventing one.

Getting started

  1. Try it without installing anything. Open openalgo.in/script and paste the HalfTrend script above into the playground.
  2. Use it in OpenAlgo. Update OpenAlgo, open the Trading page, and open the Scripts panel. Paste a script, press Save, and press play to put it on your chart.
  3. Try the EMA crossover strategy. Paste it in, press play, and read the backtest report. Change the EMA lengths and test again.
  4. Trade it in sandbox mode first. Deploy from the Strategies panel with analyzer mode on, and go live once you are comfortable with how it behaves.
  5. Building a product? Start with the specification and the npm and PyPI engines.

Learn more:

  • OpenScript documentation and playground: openalgo.in/script
  • The language specification: github.com/marketcalls/openscript
  • OpenAlgo: github.com/marketcalls/openalgo and docs.openalgo.in

posts.title: OpenAlgo CLI: Trade, Stream and Automate Your Broker from the Terminal
posts.content:
A hands-on tutorial for the new open source command line for OpenAlgo, built for scripts and AI agents

OpenAlgo already gives traders one API across 30+ brokers: REST, WebSocket, a Python SDK, MCP for AI assistants, and integrations with TradingView, Amibroker, ChartInk and Excel. Today we are adding one more way in: the OpenAlgo CLI, an open source command line tool that puts the whole OpenAlgo API in your terminal.

With one command you can check funds, pull a quote, place a sandbox order, build an option chain or stream live ticks. Every command returns clean JSON, so the same commands work in shell scripts, cron jobs, CI pipelines and, above all, AI agents.

In this tutorial we install the CLI, connect it to an OpenAlgo server, and walk through real examples. Every screenshot below comes from a live OpenAlgo instance connected to Zerodha and running in sandbox (analyzer) mode.

Source code: github.com/marketcalls/openalgo-cli (Apache 2.0)

Why a CLI?

The CLI is designed agent-first. It is not an interactive trading terminal. There are no menus or confirmation prompts. Instead:

  • Every parameter is an explicit flag such as --symbol SBIN --exchange NSE. There is nothing positional to guess.
  • Every API command prints JSON on stdout.
  • Errors are JSON on stderr, with exit codes: 0 success, 1 API error, 2 authentication error.
  • --help-all prints the full command tree, and --schema shows the response shape without calling the API, so an agent can learn the tool at runtime.
  • --dry-run on every order-changing command prints the exact request body without sending it.

That makes the CLI a natural “hands” layer for AI agents. It also makes it just as useful for traders who like to automate with a few lines of shell.

Major use cases

  1. AI agent harnesses. Give Claude Code, Codex or your own agent a shell tool and this CLI. The agent can then read positions and quotes, reason, and place or manage orders. A bundled agent skill teaches it the tool.
  2. Human-in-the-loop execution. The agent proposes an order with --dry-run, you approve the exact body, and the same body is sent.
  3. Scheduled automation. Cron jobs that square off, snapshot P&L or alert on rejected orders, each in a few lines of shell.
  4. Multiple brokers and instances. One profile per OpenAlgo instance, so one script can work across all your accounts.
  5. Research and data pipelines. Historical candles, option chains and instrument masters go straight into pandas, DuckDB or Excel with --csv.
  6. Live monitoring. Stream LTP, quotes, depth or order updates as newline-delimited JSON.
  7. Strategy operations and debugging. Start, stop and audit strategies. Use doctor, --debug and --trace to see exactly what is sent, with the API key always redacted.
  8. A universal adapter. Anything that can run a process (Excel VBA, Node, Rust, n8n) can drive OpenAlgo without an SDK.

Prerequisites

  • A running OpenAlgo server (for example http://127.0.0.1:5000) that is logged in to your broker.
  • An OpenAlgo API key, generated on the API Key page of the OpenAlgo dashboard.
  • Go is not required. The installers download a prebuilt single binary for macOS, Linux and Windows. You need Go 1.24+ only if you prefer go install or want to build from source.

Step 1: Install

macOS and Linux:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marketcalls/openalgo-cli/main/install.sh | sh

Windows (PowerShell):

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marketcalls/openalgo-cli/main/install.ps1 | iex

With Go (1.24+):

go install github.com/marketcalls/openalgo-cli/cmd/openalgo@latest

The installers detect your OS and CPU, download the latest release, verify its SHA-256 checksum and put openalgo on your path. Check the install with:

openalgo version

Step 2: Connect to your OpenAlgo server

Run openalgo profile login. It asks for the host and your API key (the key is typed without echo), validates the key against the server, and saves a profile with restricted file permissions. Then run openalgo doctor to check the whole setup:

doctor confirms that the server is reachable, which broker the key resolves to, and whether the server is in analyzer (sandbox) mode. In sandbox mode every order is simulated against live market data instead of going to your broker. That is the right place to start.

For scripts, CI and agents you can skip the profile and use environment variables, so the key never touches disk:

export OPENALGO_API_KEY=your_api_key
export OPENALGO_HOST=http://127.0.0.1:5000
openalgo account funds

Step 3: Explore the commands

Commands are grouped the way you think about trading: order, gtt, position, option, strategy, account, data, symbol, market, analyzer, stream and more. All 65 OpenAlgo REST operations are covered. Three ways to discover them:

openalgo --help-all            # every command and flag
openalgo order place --help    # one command, with examples
openalgo order list --schema   # response fields, no API call

Flags that take a fixed set of values (exchange, product, price type, action) tab-complete in bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell. Run openalgo completion zsh to set it up.

Step 4: Funds and market data

Every command prints the full OpenAlgo JSON response. The built-in --jq flag (no separate jq install needed) trims it to exactly what you need. This matters for AI agents, because fewer tokens means cheaper and faster reasoning:

openalgo account funds
openalgo data quote --symbol SBIN --exchange NSE --jq '.data.ltp'
openalgo data depth --symbol SBIN --exchange NSE
openalgo data history --symbol SBIN --exchange NSE --interval D \
  --start-date 2026-01-01 --end-date 2026-09-25 --csv > sbin.csv

Step 5: Place, check and cancel an order (safely)

First, preview the order. --dry-run builds the exact request body and prints it without sending anything. The API key is never printed.

openalgo order place --symbol SBIN --exchange NSE --action BUY --quantity 1 \
  --product CNC --pricetype LIMIT --price 950 --dry-run
openalgo order place --symbol SBIN --exchange NSE --action BUY --quantity 1 \
  --product CNC --pricetype LIMIT --price 950
openalgo order status --orderid 26092619979053
openalgo order cancel --orderid 26092619979053

Note "mode": "analyze" in the response: the order went to the sandbox, not to the exchange. A few details worth knowing:

  • Symbols use the OpenAlgo format across every broker: SBIN, BANKNIFTY24APR24FUT, NIFTY28MAR2420800CE.
  • Use CNC for equity delivery and NRML for F&O. In sandbox mode, intraday MIS orders are refused after the square-off time.
  • --strategy defaults to openalgo-cli, so CLI orders are easy to spot in your order book.
  • Rate-limited requests (HTTP 429) are retried automatically. Order-changing requests are never replayed after a server error, because a retry could place a duplicate order.

Other order types follow the same pattern: order smart, order basket, order split, order modify, gtt place, and the options order commands below.

Step 6: Options and CSV output

openalgo option symbol --underlying NIFTY --exchange NSE_INDEX \
  --expiry-date 29SEP26 --offset ATM --option-type CE
openalgo option chain --underlying NIFTY --exchange NSE_INDEX \
  --expiry-date 29SEP26 --strike-count 10 --csv > chain.csv
openalgo option greeks --symbol NIFTY29SEP2623150CE --exchange NFO

--csv turns any list (order book, positions, option chain, instruments) into a spreadsheet-ready table. Options orders resolve strikes by offset, so an ATM call buy is a single command:

openalgo option order --underlying NIFTY --exchange NSE_INDEX --expiry-date 29SEP26 \
  --offset ATM --option-type CE --action BUY --quantity 65 --product NRML

Step 7: Stream live market data

openalgo stream ltp --symbols NSE:RELIANCE,NSE:SBIN
openalgo stream quote --symbols NSE:SBIN --count 10
openalgo stream depth --symbols NSE:SBIN --depth 5 --duration 30s
openalgo stream orders

Streams print newline-delimited JSON until Ctrl-C, --count messages, or --duration. Pipe them into anything: an alerting script, a dashboard, or an agent watching order updates.

Step 8: Built for automation: schemas and structured errors

A script or agent never has to parse human text. It can branch on the exit code and read the hint to correct itself. Here is a complete end-of-day square-off job you could run from cron:

#!/bin/sh
# 15:10 IST: square off every open position and log the result
openalgo analyzer status --jq '.data.mode' >> ~/squareoff.log
openalgo position close-all --quiet >> ~/squareoff.log
openalgo account funds --jq '.data.m2mrealized' >> ~/squareoff.log

Destructive commands are truly destructive. position close-all squares off every open position, and order cancel-all cancels every open order. There are no confirmation prompts, by design, so test in sandbox mode first.

Multiple OpenAlgo instances

OpenAlgo is a single-user app, but many traders run several instances side by side, one per broker. Instance n listens on port 5000+n-1, with its WebSocket on 8765+n-1. Create one profile per instance and switch with -p:

openalgo profile login --name zerodha --host http://127.0.0.1:5000
openalgo profile login --name dhan    --host http://127.0.0.1:5001
openalgo -p zerodha position list
openalgo -p dhan account funds
openalgo -p dhan stream ltp --symbols NSE:SBIN   # ws://127.0.0.1:8766

Each profile keeps its own host and API key. A key is only ever sent to the server it belongs to.

Using the CLI with AI agents

The repository ships an agent skill at .agents/skills/openalgo-cli/SKILL.md. Load it into Claude Code, Codex or any agent that supports skills, give the agent a shell, and you can ask things like:

Check if OpenAlgo is in sandbox mode. If it is, buy 1 share of SBIN as a CNC limit order 2% below the last price, show me the dry run first, then place it and report the order status.

The agent discovers the right commands from --help, checks analyzer status, previews with --dry-run, places the order and reads the JSON response. Every step is visible and auditable in the shell history.

CLI or MCP? OpenAlgo also has an MCP server. They complement each other. The CLI is one command per call with a minimal context cost, which is ideal for harnesses, scripts and automation. MCP is a persistent tool server that suits long conversational sessions in Claude Desktop or Cursor.

Other handy commands

openalgo symbol search --query RELIANCE --exchange NSE
openalgo symbol expiry --symbol NIFTY --exchange NFO --instrumenttype options
openalgo market timings --date 2026-09-29
openalgo strategy list
openalgo api POST /funds                  # raw access to any endpoint
openalgo update                           # self-update

Get started

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marketcalls/openalgo-cli/main/install.sh | sh
openalgo profile login
openalgo doctor
  • OpenAlgo CLI on GitHub: github.com/marketcalls/openalgo-cli
  • OpenAlgo: github.com/marketcalls/openalgo
  • Documentation: docs.openalgo.in

The CLI is in alpha, and commands and flags may still change between releases. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

Disclaimer: the OpenAlgo CLI is a tool for talking to your own OpenAlgo server. Nothing in this article is investment advice. Trading involves risk; always test in sandbox mode first.

posts.title: The Cost of Building OpenAlgo
posts.content:
OpenAlgo V1.0 officially started around 8 April 2024.

At that time, it was mostly curiosity.

I had a $20 ChatGPT subscription, a bunch of ideas around trading automation, and the urge to see how far AI-assisted development could go.

There was no large engineering team.

There was no big infrastructure budget.

There was no plan to support 35+ brokers.

It simply started with:

$20 per month.

Fast forward to September 2026.

The estimated amount spent building, testing and maintaining OpenAlgo is now around:

₹44.5 lakh

But this blog is not really about that number.

It is about something I think people often misunderstand about open source.

Open source does not mean free software.

At least, not for the people building it.

The source code may be available for everyone.

You may be able to download it for free.

You may be able to modify it, study it and run it on your own machine.

But somewhere, somebody is paying the cost.

Sometimes with money.

Mostly with time.

Very often with energy.

And keeping something open source for years requires something even harder to measure:

the willpower and curiosity to keep exploring how far the project can go.

OpenAlgo is one example of that journey.

April 2024: $20 Was Enough

OpenAlgo initially started with ChatGPT 4.

The workflow was simple.

Ask ChatGPT.

Generate some code.

Understand it.

Modify it.

Test it.

Repeat.

At that stage, AI was mostly a coding assistant.

The monthly cost was approximately:

$20

For someone experimenting with software ideas, it felt almost magical.

You could suddenly attempt things that previously required much more programming effort.

But things changed quickly.

Then Came API-Based Coding

Around June 2024, I started experimenting with direct AI APIs.

OpenAI.

Anthropic.

Amazon Bedrock.

Cline inside VS Code.

This was very different from simply chatting with an AI.

The models could work with larger parts of the codebase.

They could inspect files.

Modify code.

Understand architecture.

Debug problems.

Implement larger features.

Productivity jumped enormously.

Unfortunately, so did the bill.

AI usage quickly reached around:

$20 to $40 per day

Some months were approximately:

$880

From a $20 monthly subscription to almost $900 per month within a few months.

The productivity improvement was enormous.

But everything was metered.

Every agent loop consumed tokens.

Every experiment consumed tokens.

Every wrong implementation consumed tokens.

Even asking an agent to rethink its own solution had a cost.

AI coding suddenly became incredibly powerful and incredibly expensive at the same time.

Windsurf Changed the Economics Again

Then tools such as Windsurf started offering premium plans.

For a few months, the cost of AI-assisted coding became much more predictable.

Instead of constantly thinking about token usage, I could operate at roughly:

$120 per month

That was a huge improvement.

But OpenAlgo itself was becoming much larger.

More APIs were being added.

More brokers were being integrated.

More features were being built.

More users were testing the platform.

And the biggest cost slowly stopped being AI.

It became people.

From a Personal Project to a Small Team

At some point, OpenAlgo became too large to build and maintain completely alone.

A colleague joined the development effort.

Interns were added.

That introduced another kind of work.

Explaining architecture.

Teaching how broker APIs work.

Reviewing implementations.

Testing features.

Finding edge cases.

Checking whether something that worked for one broker also worked with another.

The human development cost gradually moved to approximately:

$1,200 per month

This taught me something important.

Writing the first version of a feature is often the easy part.

Maintaining it is where the real work starts.

Then Claude Code Arrived

Claude Code pushed agentic coding another step forward.

Instead of asking AI to write isolated functions, you could assign much larger engineering tasks.

Read the repository.

Understand the issue.

Implement the change.

Run tests.

Fix failures.

Repeat.

Development speed increased again.

Claude Code added approximately another:

$400 per month

Around the same period, I started using more coding models and tools.

The broader development stack has included tools such as ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Grok.

Codex alone has been around $200 per month during recent months.

OpenCode is around $20 per month, mostly experimental.

Grok has been approximately $20 per month for around two years.

AI is no longer just a subscription.

It has effectively become part of the engineering infrastructure.

The Cost Nobody Thinks About: Brokerage

Building an algo trading platform has another unusual development expense.

Brokerage.

If you are building a normal SaaS product, testing a button may cost nothing.

If you are building a trading platform, testing a button can place a real order.

During the early stages of OpenAlgo, we were doing a lot of manual live testing.

Place an order.

Cancel it.

Modify it.

Test a market order.

Test a limit order.

Test stop loss.

Test positions.

Test holdings.

Test another exchange.

Test another broker.

Then repeat everything again.

During some of the initial months, brokerage charges were around:

₹12,000 to ₹14,000 per month

And this was not trading.

This was software testing.

Sandbox Trading Changed the Economics

Eventually, it became obvious that testing every workflow using real orders was inefficient.

So we invested heavily in building a sandbox environment.

Once sandbox testing improved, brokerage costs dropped dramatically.

Today, even with support for 35+ brokers, typical brokerage and live QA costs are closer to:

₹4,000 to ₹5,000 per month

Most development can now happen safely before touching a real broker account.

The sandbox reduced cost, risk and testing time.

It is probably one of the most valuable engineering investments we made.

But Broker APIs Never Stand Still

Broker integrations are not something you build once and forget.

APIs change.

Authentication changes.

Websocket behaviour changes.

Compliance rules change.

Exchange requirements change.

Order responses change.

A good example happened around April 2026 when brokers started implementing static IP related compliance requirements.

That triggered another round of integration work and live testing.

Brokerage expenses during that period went up to approximately:

₹24,000 in a single month

Supporting 35+ brokers does not mean writing 35 adapters once.

It means maintaining 35 moving targets.

Why We Started Doing Broker QA Audits

As OpenAlgo grew, we realised that testing itself needed better infrastructure.

So we started building structured Broker QA Audit tools.

The objective is simple:

The same OpenAlgo API should behave predictably regardless of which broker is connected underneath it.

Every broker behaves slightly differently.

Authentication is different.

Order statuses are different.

Error responses are different.

Websocket implementations are different.

Symbol formats can be different.

Rate limits are different.

Sometimes even basic interpretations of order states are different.

This is why a lot of OpenAlgo engineering work today happens in places users never see.

Regression testing.

QA audits.

Sandbox testing.

Automated validation.

Manual broker testing.

AI Made Coding Faster. Verification Became the Bottleneck.

This is probably the biggest change I have observed over the last two years.

In traditional software development, writing code was often the bottleneck.

Today AI can generate code incredibly fast.

Sometimes too fast.

An AI agent can modify 20 files before a human has properly reviewed the first five.

That creates a different engineering problem.

The bottleneck is shifting from:

Writing code

to:

Verifying code

Did the feature actually work?

Did the agent misunderstand the requirement?

Did it break another broker?

Did it introduce a security issue?

Did it handle failure conditions?

Did it only work for the happy path?

Did it silently change existing behaviour?

This is why a significant amount of our effort now goes into QA, testing and validation.

AI dramatically increased our ability to produce software.

It did not remove the need to prove that the software is correct.

Building the Software Was Only Half the Work

Another thing we gradually understood is that building a feature is not enough.

Most OpenAlgo users are traders and investors.

They come from Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities across India.

And many of them are not developers.

They may understand markets extremely well.

They may understand options, futures, technical analysis, execution, market structure or systematic trading.

But that does not necessarily mean they know Python, REST APIs, Docker, GitHub, terminals, environment variables or deployment.

That creates another responsibility.

If we build something powerful but users cannot understand how to use it, the job is only half done.

A significant amount of energy has gone into writing tutorials, improving documentation, recording videos, creating examples and explaining technical concepts in a way traders can understand.

We have also increasingly explored AI tools and assistants to help bridge this gap.

If AI can help a trader understand an API, configure a strategy, diagnose an error or learn how a feature works, then AI is not just helping us write OpenAlgo.

It is helping OpenAlgo reach more traders and investors.

That accessibility work is also part of building the platform.

Documentation Is Also Engineering

Documentation is often treated as something you do after the software is finished.

For OpenAlgo, that does not really work.

A new broker integration needs documentation.

A new API needs documentation.

A new charting feature needs documentation.

A change in authentication needs documentation.

A new sandbox workflow needs examples.

A new trading feature may need screenshots, tutorials and videos.

Sometimes the code for a feature may take a few hours.

Explaining that feature properly to thousands of users can take much longer.

And because OpenAlgo serves traders with very different technical backgrounds, documentation has to work for both ends of the spectrum.

A developer may want the exact API payload.

A trader may simply want to know:

Where do I click? What does this do? How do I know it is working?

Both are valid users.

Both matter.

Sometimes the Best Feedback Is Painful

Anyone building software publicly will eventually hear things like:

“Your software is trash.”

It is easy to dismiss comments like that.

But sometimes there is useful information hidden inside the frustration.

Maybe installation is too difficult.

Maybe the documentation is unclear.

Maybe the interface is confusing.

Maybe the user expected something obvious that we completely missed.

Maybe an important workflow takes too many steps.

Maybe technically everything works, but the experience is still poor.

So whenever someone says something is bad, I try to ask a more useful question:

What are we missing?

What frustrated this person?

What is missing from the OpenAlgo ecosystem?

Can the workflow be redesigned?

Can it be automated?

Can AI simplify it?

Can we remove another technical barrier?

Can we explain it better?

Can we build a tool that makes the problem disappear entirely?

Not every criticism will be correct.

But criticism is still data.

Sometimes the harshest feedback exposes problems that regular users quietly tolerate without ever reporting.

That feedback loop has shaped OpenAlgo continuously.

What Is Missing From the OpenAlgo Ecosystem?

This is one question I keep asking.

Not simply:

What feature should we add next?

But:

What is stopping a trader from taking an idea and turning it into a working automated trading system?

Sometimes the answer is a broker integration.

Sometimes it is charting.

Sometimes it is backtesting.

Sometimes it is risk management.

Sometimes it is alerts.

Sometimes it is a sandbox.

Sometimes it is documentation.

Sometimes it is education.

Sometimes it is simply making an existing feature easier to understand.

And increasingly we ask another question:

Can AI remove this barrier?

The purpose is not to add AI because AI is fashionable.

The purpose is to see whether technology can reduce the distance between a trader having an idea and being able to experiment with that idea.

Sometimes You Have to Leave the Laptop

Not everything can be understood from GitHub issues, analytics or online discussions.

Sometimes you have to meet people.

Over the years, I have travelled to meet developers, traders, OpenAlgo users and people from the broader ecosystem.

Those conversations are extremely valuable.

A trader sitting across the table explaining how they actually work can expose problems that may never appear in a GitHub issue.

Sometimes a requirement that initially sounds unusual makes complete sense once you understand the person’s workflow.

Sometimes users are using OpenAlgo in ways we never imagined while building the feature.

Sometimes they show exactly where the friction is.

Those conversations influence what gets built next.

OpenAlgo is not shaped only by code.

It is shaped by listening to traders.

Understanding their pain.

Understanding their requirements.

Watching how they actually use the platform.

And trying to make OpenAlgo a little better every single day.

Travel, conversations and community engagement are also part of the cost of building OpenAlgo.

They are simply much harder to represent in a spreadsheet.

Infrastructure Is a Continuous Expense

OpenAlgo also requires servers and development infrastructure.

Our average server and infrastructure cost is approximately:

₹10,000 per month

Across roughly 30 months, that alone is around:

₹3 lakh

Then there is the hardware used for development.

Computers and related hardware have cost approximately:

₹3.5 lakh

These are easy costs to overlook when calculating the cost of open-source software.

GitHub may be free.

The source code may be free.

The infrastructure required to continuously develop and test that software is not.

Even Communication Has Infrastructure

Another unusual cost is content and communication.

We built tools such as Sketchmaker to help create visual content for social media.

The infrastructure and APIs behind that cost approximately:

₹5,000 per month

Across 30 months:

₹1.5 lakh

Medium, Cloudflare and other smaller publishing services add another recurring cost.

Individually, these numbers look small.

Over multiple years, everything adds up.

Rough Cost of Building OpenAlgo

As of September 2026, the approximate expenditure looks something like this:

These are approximate numbers.

Some months were much cheaper.

Some months were significantly more expensive.

There are also smaller expenses that are not included.

Travel, events, education, community interaction and various operational expenses are not fully represented here.

One Very Important Cost Is Missing

My own time.

From April 2024 until today, a huge number of hours have gone into coding, testing, documentation, broker integrations, debugging, community support, reviewing pull requests, experimenting with AI tools, building infrastructure, recording videos, writing tutorials, travelling to meet users and simply observing how traders actually use OpenAlgo.

I have intentionally not assigned a monetary value to that time.

If I did, the true economic cost of OpenAlgo would be significantly higher.

And time is only one part of it.

Open source requires energy.

You build something.

Someone finds an issue.

You fix it.

Someone requests another broker.

You explore it.

A broker changes its API.

You revisit old code.

Someone contributes a pull request.

You review it.

A regulatory change happens.

A dependency changes.

An AI agent introduces a regression.

Someone says the software is terrible.

You investigate whether they discovered something you missed.

You improve it.

And you keep going.

That cycle never really ends.

Then Why Are We Spending This Much on Something Free?

This is probably the obvious question.

If OpenAlgo costs real money to build and maintain, what is the business model?

When will subscriptions start?

When will investors come in?

When will brokers sponsor it?

When will the free version disappear?

We have been asked versions of these questions almost from the beginning.

And we answered them publicly very early in the journey.

On 6 July 2024, only a few months after OpenAlgo officially started, I published our commitment to the community.

The position was simple:

OpenAlgo would remain free and open source for retail users.

More than two years later, that commitment has not changed.

And we intend to continue with it.

OpenAlgo Is Not a VC-Funded Company

OpenAlgo is not being built with the objective of becoming another venture-funded fintech startup.

We are not preparing a pitch deck.

We are not trying to raise VC funding.

We are not chasing valuation.

We are not building towards an eventual funding round.

OpenAlgo is self-funded and bootstrapped.

That gives us something extremely valuable:

freedom to decide what OpenAlgo should become.

We can explore ideas because they are interesting.

We can build something because traders need it.

We can spend weeks solving a technical problem without having to justify whether it improves quarterly revenue.

Not everything has to become a business model.

Sometimes curiosity itself is enough reason to build.

Why We Declined Broker Sponsorships

As OpenAlgo grew, brokers approached us with sponsorship opportunities.

Good brokers.

Serious offers.

We declined them.

That was a conscious decision.

OpenAlgo sits between traders and brokers.

If one broker starts funding the project, even with the best intentions, questions naturally arise.

Does that broker receive priority?

Does their integration get more attention?

Are recommendations influenced?

Will another broker be treated differently?

Even the perception of that conflict matters.

So we decided that OpenAlgo should remain:

broker neutral.

We integrate brokers because traders use them.

We fix broker integrations because users need them.

We should be able to say that without someone wondering whether money influenced the decision.

That independence is worth protecting.

Users Have Offered Us Money Too

Users who found OpenAlgo useful have also offered financial support.

We are grateful for that gesture.

But we declined those offers too.

What helps an open-source project most is participation.

A trader who identifies a reproducible problem and provides screenshots, logs and context can save hours of investigation.

Someone who improves a tutorial or documentation can help hundreds of other users.

Someone who tests a new release can uncover issues before they affect the wider community.

And developers can contribute code where they have the knowledge and time to do so.

OpenAlgo now has 85+ contributors, which is a great sign of how much the ecosystem has grown.

But growth creates another challenge.

There can be 150+ pull requests waiting to be reviewed, tested or approved.

Code contributions themselves also require maintenance energy.

Every significant change has to be understood, tested for regressions, checked for security implications and sometimes validated across multiple brokers.

Open source works best when contribution is viewed not only as submitting code, but as sharing the responsibility of making the software better.

Broker Neutrality Matters to Us

Supporting 35+ brokers makes independence especially important.

Our objective is not to tell traders which broker they should use.

Our objective is to provide a common technology layer where traders can choose their broker and still use the same OpenAlgo ecosystem.

One broker may have better APIs.

Another may have different features.

Another may suit a particular trader better.

Those are decisions traders should make themselves.

Our job is to make OpenAlgo work as predictably as possible across them.

That is why we want to remain independent.

No broker sponsorship deciding our roadmap.

No VC telling us what needs to be monetized.

No investor asking which feature generates revenue.

Just users, contributors, technology and curiosity shaping the direction of the project.

Our July 2024 Commitment Still Stands

When we published our commitment in July 2024, OpenAlgo was still young.

It is easy to make promises when a project is small and inexpensive.

The real test comes when the project grows.

More than two years have passed.

The codebase has grown.

The number of brokers has grown.

The community has grown.

Development costs have grown.

Infrastructure costs have grown.

The complexity of maintaining OpenAlgo has grown enormously.

But our position remains the same.

OpenAlgo remains open source.

OpenAlgo remains free for retail users.

We remain self-funded and bootstrapped.

We are not planning to raise VC funding for OpenAlgo.

We continue to remain broker neutral.

That is not a position we created recently because it sounds good.

It is something we stated publicly in July 2024 and have continued to follow as the project expanded.

Open Source Is Free to Use. It Is Not Free to Build.

This is really the reason I wanted to write this article.

When people hear “open source”, there is sometimes an assumption that open source means free software.

For the user, it often is.

For the creator, it almost never is.

There is money involved.

There is infrastructure involved.

There are machines involved.

There are API bills.

There are developers.

There is testing.

There is documentation.

There are tutorials.

There are videos.

There is community support.

There is travel.

But above all, there is time and energy.

Keeping a project open source requires another ingredient.

Willpower.

You have to genuinely enjoy exploring the problem.

You have to remain curious enough to keep pushing the limits.

You have to be willing to share what you build even when keeping everything private might sometimes be easier.

And you need enough conviction to continue doing it even when monetizing, taking sponsorships or raising capital might be the easier path.

That curiosity and independence are probably what have kept OpenAlgo moving from a small experiment into what it is today.

AI Reduced the Cost of Ambition

AI made it possible for a very small team to build something that would previously have required a much larger engineering organisation.

That represents an enormous reduction in the cost of software creation.

But something interesting happens when productivity increases.

You do not necessarily spend less.

You start building more.

Instead of building five features, you build fifty.

Instead of supporting five brokers, you try supporting thirty-five.

Instead of stopping with an API layer, you start building charts, sandbox systems, risk management, alerts, voice agents, QA tools, documentation systems and developer infrastructure.

AI reduced the cost of ambition.

And when ambition becomes cheaper, the boundaries of the project expand.

The Most Expensive Part Is No Longer Code

If there is one thing I have learned from building OpenAlgo, it is this:

The cost of producing code is collapsing.

But the cost of trust is not.

Neither is the cost of understanding your users.

You still have to test the software.

You still have to audit it.

You still have to understand it.

You still have to document it.

You still have to explain it.

You still have to listen when users tell you something is wrong.

You still have to maintain it.

And when that software interacts with real trading accounts and real money, correctness matters far more than how quickly the code was generated.

OpenAlgo started as a $20 experiment.

What keeps it moving today is not just money.

It is curiosity, time, energy, independence and a community willing to participate.

Our commitment from July 2024 still stands.

Open source may be free to use.

It is never free to build.

posts.title: AI Couldn’t Build Serious Software. Then Coding Agents Arrived
posts.content:
This is how early technology looks.

When we started building OpenAlgo around 2024, there were no coding agents in the way we understand them today.

We were mostly using ChatGPT.

Copy some code.

Paste it into ChatGPT.

Explain the problem.

Get some code back.

Paste it into the editor.

Run it.

Find the error.

Go back to ChatGPT.

Repeat.

At the time, a common reaction was:

“You can build small scripts with AI, but you cannot build large software.”

“AI-generated code will become impossible to maintain.”

“ChatGPT doesn’t understand the entire codebase.”

“You still need to write most of the serious code yourself.”

And they were right about one thing.

The technology was not ready yet.

Context windows were limited.

Models forgot earlier decisions.

Large refactoring was painful.

Debugging required constant human intervention.

There was no agent sitting inside your repository, reading files, running tests, executing commands, checking errors and iterating on its own.

But something important was already visible.

Potential.

For the first time, I could describe what I wanted to build in plain English and have AI help me turn that idea into working software.

It didn’t matter that I had to copy and paste code.

It didn’t matter that the model occasionally hallucinated functions.

It didn’t matter that I had to fix things manually.

The direction was obvious.

Then came coding agents.

Cursor.

Claude Code.

Codex.

And now we have tons of agent harnesses that can explore repositories, write code, run commands, execute tests, debug failures, refactor multiple files and keep iterating toward a goal.

The workflow itself has changed.

2024:

Human writes prompts.
AI writes snippets.
Human copies, integrates, tests and fixes.

2026:

Human defines intent, architecture and constraints.
Agents explore, implement, test, debug and iterate.
Humans increasingly review, steer and make engineering decisions.

That is a very different way of building software.

And I don’t think we are anywhere close to the end of this transition.

Today people still point at agent-generated code that is messy, inefficient or occasionally ridiculous and conclude:

“AI cannot build serious software.”

Maybe.

But that reminds me of looking at early AI-generated images with six fingers and concluding that machines would never generate realistic images.

The flaws are real.

But the trajectory matters more.

The interesting question isn’t:

“Can an AI agent build perfect production software today?”

The more interesting question is:

“If coding agents have progressed this much in just a couple of years, what will software development look like five years from now?”

OpenAlgo has given me a front-row seat to this transition.

We started with ChatGPT-assisted coding.

Then moved into agent-assisted development.

Now we are increasingly thinking about software development as orchestrating agents, tools, tests, skills, context and workflows.

The role of the developer is changing with it.

Less time may eventually be spent typing every line of code.

More time will be spent defining what should be built, designing systems, providing context, setting constraints, testing assumptions, reviewing outputs and coordinating agents.

This is how early technology looks.

Imperfect.

Flawed.

Sometimes ridiculous.

But full of possibilities for those curious enough to look beyond what it can do today and imagine what it is becoming.

posts.title: OpenAlgo Charts — A charting engine you actually own
posts.content:
OpenAlgo Charts is a from-scratch, dependency-free HTML5-canvas charting engine: 13 chart types plus six transforms, 90+ indicators, 43 drawing tools, order flow, and live on-chart trading: 37 KB Brotli for the base engine, and nothing you don’t import.

Every trading app hits the same wall. The chart is the product, the place where the user spends the whole session, and yet it is the one piece most teams rent. You pick a vendor library, accept its licence, accept its bundle size, accept the features it decided you needed, and then spend weeks bending it into something that looks like yours.

OpenAlgo Charts starts from the other end. It is original code, written from scratch for the OpenAlgo ecosystem, with zero runtime dependencies and a permissive licence. You read it, fork it, ship it inside a commercial product, and nobody sends you an invoice for a seat.

What it is

One canvas pipeline per pane. No SVG, no DOM node per bar, no framework underneath, which is why the whole thing stays small and stays smooth when the data gets long. The time axis is gapless by default, so weekends, holidays and session breaks collapse instead of leaving dead space in the middle of your chart.

The library ships as six tiers you import separately: the base engine, indicators, drawing tools, transforms, profiles and order flow, and trading. Each tier registers itself into the base engine’s registries, so a feature you never import costs you exactly nothing. Everything together is 74.2 KB Brotli, and the budget is enforced in CI: there are no runtime dependencies to exclude from the measurement.

The feature tour

Chart types. Candles, hollow and volume candles, OHLC bars, high-low, line, line with markers, step, area, HLC area, baseline, columns and histogram. On top of those sit the transforms traders ask for by name: Heikin Ashi, Renko, Range bars, Line Break, Point & Figure with fixed, percent or ATR box sizing, and Kagi.

Indicators. Twenty built in: SMA, EMA, WMA, VWAP, Bollinger Bands, Supertrend, HalfTrend, Parabolic SAR, Ichimoku Cloud, RSI, MACD, Stochastic, ADX/DMI, CCI, MFI, ATR, William VIX FIX, Volume, OBV and A/D. The chart owns the whole lifecycle: pane placement, reference levels, fixed ranges like RSI’s 0 to 100, recompute on new data, teardown. Colour, opacity, thickness and line style come free on every plot, generated from the indicator’s own descriptor. Indicators whose input isn’t OHLCV (open interest, cumulative delta, anything from an external feed) get a separate contract built for exactly that.

Drawing tools. Forty-three of them: trend lines and rays, rectangles and ellipses, paths and curves, parallel and Fibonacci channels, retracements, extensions, time zones, speed fans, Gann fan and box, cyclic and sine lines, long and short position tools with risk/reward and risk-based sizing, price and date range measurers, text, callouts, flags, brush and highlighter. Anchors are stored as time and price, never pixels, so a drawing survives zoom, resolves inside collapsed session gaps, and still holds past the last bar. Magnet snap, per-anchor dragging, undo/redo where a whole drag counts as one step, and persistence are all in the box.

Profiles and order flow. Volume Profile, Market Profile (TPO), Footprint and cumulative delta: the analysis layer most open libraries simply don’t have.

Trading on the chart itself

This is the part that turns a chart into a terminal. Order, position and bracket lines with live P&L. One-click placement and drag-to-modify. OCO, validation, and a real order state machine behind it rather than a pile of callbacks. A depth-of-market ladder from 5 to 200 levels. And an analyzer mode, a sandbox where every action behaves exactly as it will live, but nothing leaves your machine until you arm it.

The data underneath is OpenAlgo-native: REST history plus WebSocket ticks with auto-reconnect and resubscribe, live candle aggregation, tick and volume bars, event markers for earnings, dividends and expiry, and one unified event bus for the lot. Any other broker fits behind a small data-feed adapter.

This is not a library looking for its first user. It runs inside the OpenAlgo open-source application itself, doing the heavy lifting for chart-based trading, custom technical indicators and drawing, across the 35+ brokers OpenAlgo now supports. Every rough edge gets found there first.

For developers: building on top

The design rule is registries, not switches. Chart types, indicators and drawing tools are all descriptors, so adding one is a registration, never a change to the core. Write your own indicator and it inherits the same settings UI, the same pane handling, the same styling controls as the built-ins. Write your own overlay against the primitive API and you are using the same interface that markers, trading lines and profiles are built on. There is no privileged internal layer you can’t reach.

The drawing layer is deliberately headless: placement, selection, dragging, snapping and undo are handled, but there is no toolbar and no dialog. You supply the chrome, in your own design language, and the engine never fights you for it.

Layouts are one JSON payload. A single call captures viewport, grid, panes, price scales, indicator instances and drawings; another restores them. Saved templates and per-user workspaces need no extra storage plumbing on your side.

And it is readable. A few thousand lines of commented TypeScript with a documented architecture, 620 unit tests across 50 files, strict typechecking, and a full docs site where every code sample on the page is a live chart running the real library. No minified vendor blob to reverse-engineer when something behaves oddly at 3am.

It teaches your AI assistant, too

The repository ships six agent skills: a reference hub with 18 deep-dive files covering the whole API surface and its foot-guns, plus task skills for scaffolding a chart, adding indicators, building a terminal, writing a plugin and debugging. One command installs them into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, Gemini CLI and the rest. Your assistant stops guessing at the API and starts using it.

If you trade or invest

You get a terminal that runs on your own data and your own machine. Your broker connection stays yours; your chart layouts stay on your disk. Study a setup with Renko or Point & Figure, mark it up with a Fibonacci retracement, size the trade with the position tool’s risk-based sizing, then place the order from the chart without switching windows, and rehearse the whole thing in analyzer mode first.

Because the profile and order-flow tier is included rather than sold as an add-on, volume profile, market profile and cumulative delta are simply there. So is the depth ladder. For anyone who has been paying a monthly subscription for exactly that shortlist, the arithmetic is worth doing.

If you run a small broker or a fintech business

Charting is usually the line item that decides whether a retail platform is viable. Per-seat licensing scales with your user count, which means your best growth month is also your worst margin month. An Apache-2.0 engine removes that coupling entirely: your charting cost is engineering time, not a function of how many clients you onboard.

It is also yours to brand. Themes, chrome and layout are all your code, so the terminal looks like your product rather than a vendor’s widget with your logo in the corner. Thirty-seven kilobytes for the base engine matters when your customers trade from mid-range phones on patchy mobile data. And when a client asks how the P&L on their screen was computed, you can show them the file, a conversation that is very hard to have about a closed dependency.

A small team can go from history endpoint to a branded, order-capable terminal without a procurement cycle, a sales call, or a renewal negotiation eighteen months later.

The licence, in plain English

Apache-2.0. Use it commercially. Modify it. Ship it inside a closed-source product. Keep your changes private if you want to. No per-seat fee, no revenue share, no non-commercial asterisk, no attribution gymnastics beyond keeping the licence and NOTICE file with the code and flagging files you changed. It also grants you a patent licence from every contributor, which is the clause your legal reviewer will actually care about.

What it does not give you is a warranty or a support contract; the code ships as is. For a piece of infrastructure you can read end to end, that is a reasonable trade.

Version 1.0.29 is honest about its gaps, and the README lists them: footprint and order flow need trade-by-trade data classified bid/ask, so it is live-session-only unless you add a tick recorder; most profile primitives are dark-tuned and need explicit colours on a light theme; percentage and indexed-to-100 price scales are not implemented; and the optional DOM chrome package (toolbar, dialogs, command palette, objects panel) is the next planned piece, so today that UI lives in the examples.

Getting started

Install it from npm with npm install openalgo-charts, then read the docs and click through the live example gallery at marketcalls.github.io/openalgo-charts.

The source, the architecture document and the runnable demos are at github.com/marketcalls/openalgo-charts.

If you are building something on it, whether an indicator, a plugin or a whole terminal, come and say so in the OpenAlgo community at openalgo.in/discord. That is where the roadmap gets decided.

posts.title: Harness Engineering Explain in Simple Terms
posts.content:
AI development is moving through clear phases.

2023: Prompt Engineering — telling AI what to do
2024: Context Engineering — giving AI the right information
2025: Agentic Engineering — letting AI plan and act
2026: Harness Engineering — making AI prove the work is safe and correct

A large language model by itself is just raw intelligence. It can answer questions, write code, summarize text, or reason through a problem. But on its own, it is still only an API call. You give it tokens, and it gives back tokens.

To make it useful in the real world, we need to put a system around it.

That system is the harness.

A harness gives the AI tools, context, permissions, memory, execution rules, test runners, logs, safety checks, and verification loops. It turns the model from a smart chatbot into a working agent.

This is why the same model can feel very different in different tools. A model inside Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot, or a custom company agent may behave differently because the harness around the model is different. The model is only one part of the experience. The harness decides how the model sees files, calls tools, runs commands, manages context, asks permission, tests output, and completes work.

Prompt engineering is still useful, but it only tells the AI what to do.

Context engineering is also important, because it gives the AI the right files, docs, database results, or project information at the right time.

Agentic engineering lets the AI take action using tools.

But harness engineering goes one level above all of this. It controls the full workflow.

A good harness does not simply ask the AI to “build a feature.” It puts the AI inside a loop:

Plan → Do one task → Test → Verify → Log → Move to the next task

This loop matters because long-running AI tasks often fail silently. The agent may assume something is finished when it is not. It may skip testing. It may forget earlier decisions after context summarization. It may produce a half-working feature where some buttons work and some do not.

Harness engineering reduces this problem by making the AI work in controlled steps.

For example, in a coding workflow, a harness can force the agent to:

  • read the requirement
  • break it into smaller tasks
  • pick one task at a time
  • edit the code
  • run tests
  • verify the output
  • log the result
  • continue only after checks pass

This is not just automation. It is controlled execution.

In OpenAlgo terms, if we use a SKILL.md to guide an AI agent on how to integrate a new broker, that is scaffolding. It helps the agent understand the folder structure, API format, order parameters, websocket rules, safety checklist, and coding conventions.

But the broker test suite, mock broker API, sandbox mode, order validation, websocket replay tests, CI checks, logging, and live-order safety blocks are harness engineering.

That is the key difference:

Scaffolding helps build it correctly.
Harness engineering proves it works safely.

This is especially important in trading systems, finance, coding agents, automation tools, and any system where the AI can take real actions. In these areas, we cannot trust output just because it looks correct. The work must be tested, validated, logged, and verified.

A strong harness can include:

  • tool calling
  • context management
  • permission controls
  • sandbox execution
  • mock testing
  • validation rules
  • retries
  • logs
  • human approval
  • final verification

This is also why companies may start building their own internal harnesses. General-purpose tools like Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, or Copilot are useful for broad coding tasks. But a company-specific harness can be much more powerful for repeated internal workflows.

For example, a trading platform may need a harness that understands broker APIs, order safety, mock trades, symbol mapping, exchange rules, and strict no-live-order testing. A normal coding agent may not know these rules deeply enough. A custom harness can enforce them.

So harness engineering is not just a buzzword. It is the next layer of AI engineering.

We are moving from asking AI to do work, to building systems that make AI’s work verifiable.

Prompt engineering made AI useful.
Context engineering made AI informed.
Agentic engineering made AI actionable.
Harness engineering makes AI reliable.

posts.title: OpenGreeks: Fast Options Pricing and Greeks for Python, Powered by Rust
posts.content:
How we rebuilt vollib in Rust and shrank a full NIFTY option chain refresh from 9 ms to 0.3 ms, with bit-for-bit identical Greeks.

If you have ever built an Indian options analytics engine in Python, the story usually goes like this. You start with py_vollib or vollib because it is the canonical reference for Black-76, Black-Scholes and Black-Scholes-Merton. The math is correct, the API is clean, and the textbook anchors from Hull and Haug all pass.

Then you scale up.

You move from a single quote to a full NIFTY chain. Then to BANKNIFTY plus FINNIFTY. Then to live tick refresh at 5 Hz, then 10 Hz, then 20 Hz. Somewhere along that path, your CPU starts melting and your event loop starts skipping ticks. Profile in hand, you discover that you are spending almost all of your budget inside py_lets_be_rational and scipy.stats.norm.cdf.

This is the wall that OpenGreeks was built to break. And Now integrated inside openalgo.

What OpenGreeks is

OpenGreeks is a drop-in replacement for vollib and py_vollib where the Black-76, Black-Scholes, and Black-Scholes-Merton pricing and Greeks paths are reimplemented in zero-dependency Rust and exposed to Python through PyO3.

Two design constraints shaped everything else.

First, the public API matches py_vollib exactly. Same function names, same argument order, same scaling conventions (vega multiplied by 0.01, theta divided by 365, rho multiplied by 0.01). Migration is one line:

# before
from py_vollib.black.greeks.analytical import delta, gamma, vega, theta, rho
# after
from opengreeks.black76 import delta, gamma, vega, theta, rho

Second, the math has to be byte-identical where possible. Not “close enough.” Bit-for-bit. A trading desk cannot adopt a new pricing library if it might disagree with the reference on the third decimal of delta. So we validated 29 edge cases against vollib==1.0.7:

GreekMax abs error vs vollibdelta, gamma, vega, theta, rho0.0e+00 (bit-for-bit identical)price1.4e-12 (relative 1.7e-14, around 14 digits)IV (well-conditioned)8.6e-10

The Greeks are not “approximately equal.” They are equal.

The speed numbers

These are measured on a single laptop core against vollib==1.0.7, reproduced in bench/bench_parity.py:

The headline that matters for retail and prop desks running in India: a full NIFTY option chain refresh of roughly 200 options, computing all five Greeks plus implied volatility, drops from about 9 ms in vollib to about 0.3 ms in OpenGreeks. That is the difference between saturating one CPU core at 100 Hz and using about 3 percent of that core for the same workload.

Why Rust, and why now

Pricing math is the textbook case for a native extension. The work is CPU bound, the inputs and outputs are simple floats, and the inner loop is dominated by exp, log, and erf calls. Python pays a per-call interpreter tax for every one of these, and py_vollib was built across multiple pure-Python packages that recurse through several layers before reaching the numerical kernel.

Rust gives us three things that matter here:

  1. No interpreter overhead on the hot path. Once you cross the PyO3 boundary, the entire pricing loop runs at native speed.
  2. Zero runtime dependencies in the core. black76_rust and bsm_rust use only the standard library math functions. No scipy, no pandas, no cody_special shared object that fails to load on minimal Python distros.
  3. Vectorisation through NumPy in one boundary crossing. The *_array variants take a NumPy array in, run the entire chain inside a tight Rust loop, and return a NumPy array out. You pay the PyO3 cost once, not 200 times.

That last point is the one that converts “fast scalar” into “stupid fast on a chain.”

The dependency story

This part rarely gets discussed but it matters a lot in production.

PackageRuntime dependenciespip install vollibpy_lets_be_rational, cody_special, piecewise_rational, simplejson, numpy, pandas, scipypip install opengreeksnumpy

If you have ever shipped a vollib-based service into a slim container or a corporate Python environment, you have probably hit a _testcapi import error from cody_special or a wheel-build failure on scipy on Python 3.13. OpenGreeks ships prebuilt wheels for Linux, macOS, and Windows on every supported CPython and PyPy, and the only thing it asks of the host environment is NumPy.

Using it

Black-76 (futures, NIFTY style)

from opengreeks.black76 import (
    black, implied_volatility, delta, gamma, vega, theta, rho,
)
F, K, t, r, sigma = 22000.0, 22000.0, 30 / 365, 0.07, 0.18
price = black('c', F, K, t, r, sigma)                  # 450.27
iv    = implied_volatility(price, F, K, r, t, 'c')     # 0.18
d     = delta('c', F, K, t, r, sigma)
g     = gamma('c', F, K, t, r, sigma)
v     = vega ('c', F, K, t, r, sigma)
th    = theta('c', F, K, t, r, sigma)
rh    = rho  ('c', F, K, t, r, sigma)

Black-Scholes and Black-Scholes-Merton

from opengreeks.black_scholes import black_scholes
from opengreeks.black_scholes_merton import black_scholes_merton
bs  = black_scholes('c', 100.0, 90.0, 0.5, 0.01, 0.20)             # 12.111581
bsm = black_scholes_merton('p', 100.0, 95.0, 0.5, 0.10, 0.20, 0.05)  # 2.4648 (Haug p.4)

Whole-chain refresh

For real workloads, use the *_array variants. One PyO3 hop, one Rust loop, NumPy in and out:

import numpy as np
from opengreeks import black76
K = np.linspace(20000.0, 24000.0, 200)
F = np.full_like(K, 22000.0)
t = np.full_like(K, 30 / 365)
s = np.full_like(K, 0.18)
prices = black76.black_array('c', F, K, t, 0.07, s)
ivs    = black76.implied_volatility_array(prices, F, K, 0.07, t, 'c')
deltas = black76.delta_array('c', F, K, t, 0.07, s)

This is the call path that does a chain refresh in 0.3 ms.

What it does not try to be

OpenGreeks is intentionally narrow at v0.1.0. It does Black-76, Black-Scholes, and Black-Scholes-Merton, the three models that cover 99 percent of vanilla European-style options pricing on Indian and US equity, index, and futures markets. It does not yet ship Heston, SABR, American or Bermudan exercise, or volatility surface fitting.

Those are planned as additional <model>_rust/ crates and opengreeks.<model> submodules, slotted in without breaking the published API. The point of v0.1.0 is to nail the parity story on the most-used pricing kernels first.

Credits

OpenGreeks would not exist without py_vollib and vollib by Gammon Capital LLC (MIT-licensed). Their function names, argument orders, and scaling conventions are reused verbatim, because the entire value proposition of OpenGreeks is that you can pip install opengreeks, change one import line, and keep all the surrounding analytics code that you already wrote against vollib.

The numerical kernels stand on the shoulders of Peter Jaeckel’s “Let’s Be Rational” IV inversion (jaeckel.org), W. J. Cody’s rational Chebyshev approximations for erf (Math. Comp. 1969), A. R. Wichura’s Algorithm AS 241 inverse normal CDF (Appl. Stat. 1988), and the Hull and Haug textbook validation anchors.

Try it

pip install opengreeks

Repo, benchmark scripts, and the full parity report are at:

github.com/marketcalls/opengreeks

If you are running a live options analytics workload on vollib or py_vollib today, the migration is one line and you get back about 95 percent of the CPU you were spending on pricing math. Give it a swap and tell us what your chain refresh latency drops to.
